bio.en: Ramesh Johari is a professor at Stanford University focused on the design and operation of online marketplaces, and has advised and worked with many of the world's largest marketplaces including Airbnb, Uber, Stripe, Bumble, and Stitch Fix.
bio.zh: Ramesh Johari 是斯坦福大学教授，研究方向为在线市场的设计与运营，曾为包括 Airbnb、Uber、Stripe、Bumble 和 Stitch Fix 在内的全球最大的一批市场平台提供咨询与合作。

summary.en: Ramesh reframes marketplace businesses around the goal of achieving 'scaled liquidity' on both sides of the platform, and warns that most perceived problems are not marketplace-specific at all. He explains how data science should shift from machine learning to causal inference to truly improve matching and ranking, and why a culture of fast, learning-oriented experiments beats waiting for statistical significance. The conversation is a deep, nerdy dive into building thriving marketplaces.
summary.zh: Ramesh 将市场业务重新定义为追求平台双边“规模化流动性（scaled liquidity）”的目标，并提醒说，大多数看似的问题根本不是市场特有的。他解释了数据科学应当从机器学习转向因果推断，才能真正改善匹配与排序，以及为什么“快速、以学习为导向的实验文化”优于苦等统计显著性。本期是对打造繁荣市场平台的深度、硬核剖析。

turns.en: Marketplaces are a little bit like a game of whac-a-mole. One example that I came across with one of the companies I worked with that I love is our new supply side was having a pretty bad experience. (00:00:12): So what we decided to do is build some custom bespoke features that were really going to direct them to more experienced folks on the other side of the market. Good. And then, yeah, lo and behold, pretty soon those metrics start to look better. But then we're looking at it, we're like, "Wait a second. Now the existing folks on the other side are having a worse experience," so you kind of whiplash around. You're like, "Oh, wait a second. We better do something about that." So we take them, we try to match them up with the more experienced folks, and now suddenly a month after that, you're like, "Wait a second," and your metrics just keep moving around. And that's because the whac-a-mole game here is ultimately, a lot of marketplace management is moving attention and inventory around. Many of the changes that are most consequential create winners and losers. And rolling with those changes is about recognizing whether the winners you've created are more important to your business than the losers you've created in the process.
turns.zh: 市场平台有点像打地鼠的游戏。我曾在合作的一家公司遇到过一个例子，当时我们的新供应商端遇到了相当糟糕的体验。（00:00:12）所以我们决定开发一些定制功能，引导他们与市场另一端更有经验的合作伙伴对接。效果不错。然而很快，相关指标开始好转。但当我们回头看时，发现另一端的现有合作伙伴体验反而更差了——这就像被突然打脸。我们不得不迅速调整，试图将他们与更资深的合作伙伴匹配。结果一个月后，指标又开始波动。这是因为市场管理本质上就是在调配注意力和库存资源。许多关键变革都会产生赢家和输家。要适应这些变化，就必须判断你创造的赢家对业务的价值，是否比过程中产生的输家更重要。

turns.zh: 让我们先从宏观层面入手，奠定一些基础。你对市场平台业务的定义很独特。拉梅什，请问什么是市场平台业务？为什么数据对构建成功的市场平台业务如此重要，又是不可或缺的组成部分？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: It's interesting when people sit down and think about, say Airbnb, what does Airbnb sell? Average person is like, "That's pretty obvious. Airbnb sells rooms. I go there to book a room I want to stay at," right? Other people say, "What does Uber sell? Uber sells me rides. I'd use Uber when I need to get a ride from somewhere to somewhere else." (00:06:10): And in some sense, you're not wrong. I mean, you go there. That's a platform to get these things. But that's not what the platform is selling. That's a really important distinction. There are people on the platform that are selling that to you. The hosts on Airbnb are selling you listings. The drivers on Uber are selling you rides. But Uber and Airbnb are selling you the taking away of something, which is a weird thing to think about. What they're taking away is the friction of finding a place to stay. They're taking away the friction of finding a driver. (00:06:42): In economics, we call those things transaction costs. When you take econ 1, you learn about markets and how supply meets demand, and we get prices out of that. But what you don't learn until econ 201 is that markets don't always work. And one of the reasons markets don't always work is because we have what are called market failures due to the presence of these kinds of friction. So what's a market failure? It's that Lenny wants to get from Palo Alto to Burlingame and he can't do it. Why can't he do it? He doesn't have anyone to drive him. Well, why doesn't he just call someone to drive him? Well, who's he supposed to call? Who are those people? Are they out there? Are they willing to drive him right now, right at 10:00 AM on a Friday? Are they willing to take him somewhere? (00:07:22): When I want to stay somewhere when I'm traveling, a friction is, who's willing to give me their room? I mean on principle, there's people who are willing to let me stay in their living room, but I don't know who they are. (00:07:31): So those are frictions, and what the marketplaces are selling you is taking the friction away. That's what you're paying them for. And it's an important observation, because what that means is the marketplace's customers aren't just the people buying the rides, they're buying the listings. Actually, the hosts are Airbnb's customers, and the drivers are also Uber's customers. So both sides of the marketplace are the customers of the platform. Both sides depend on the platform to help the platform take that friction away. Because just like you want a place to stay or you want to ride, the driver is at Uber because he wants to earn money by taking people places. And the host is on Airbnb because they want to earn money by selling their listing. (00:08:10): I think this concept that we're making money by taking transaction costs away is such a fundamental idea that's misunderstood around marketplaces. That when you're an entrepreneur starting a marketplace or thinking about your business model, I think you can be wildly off if you forget that that's the thing that's fundamentally your value proposition. And then you asked about the role of data, and more broadly data science in marketplaces. (00:08:36): So it's an interesting thing, right? The example I always love to give are the ancient Agoras in Greece or Trajan's Market in Rome. When you look at pictures of these things, what really stands out to me is the rock. I mean, these things are made of stone. It's not like you were going to move a booth from one place to another place without moving a lot of rock from one place to another place. (00:09:00): So you flash forward to 2023, and here we are with technology undergirding pretty much every kind of commerce now. And it means we can architect and re-architect the marketplace kind of on the fly, and we really are doing it all the time. (00:09:14): And these frictions that are getting taken away, they're getting taken away because of data and data science. So I really want to highlight three pieces of this for people, which I want you to think of them as a cycle. But to start with, let's just lay them out one at a time. (00:09:29): One of them is finding people to match with. So that's the problem of, "I want to stay somewhere. Who is out there, who's willing to let me stay with them on a given timeframe?" And then if I'm a host, I have a listing. Who is out there, who's willing to stay at my place when I have it available? So that's finding matches. (00:09:49): Then there's making the match. And so here, going back to my time at oDesk, a big problem that we dealt with there was if I've got multiple applicants to my job, who should I hire? Who should I interview? It's a common problem we face in the real world, but now it's all remote. I don't meet these people in person. All I've got is this application they submitted to me. I need help triaging that. Okay? So that's helping make a match out of possible partners you can match with. (00:10:16): And then finally, we make matches. Well, what do the matches tell us, right? I mean, if you stay somewhere in Airbnb, you learn something about the host, you learn something about the listing. The host learns about you too. And that's all information that the marketplace should feed back in. So this is where we get to rating systems and feedback systems, even passive data collection, right? Did you leave your booking before you were supposed to leave? Well, maybe that's a sign that something didn't quite work out the way you wanted to work out. So that's passive data collection. Did you leave five stars? That's active data collection. (00:10:47): Get all this back in, and what does that do? Well, that lets us do a better job finding potential matches and make potential matches in the future. Every single thing I just said, finding potential matches, making matches, and then learning about those matches, and then cycling back again, that is the data science in marketplaces. (00:11:05): And I feel like every marketplace that you could think of in any vertical has those three problems to deal with and relies on algorithms in data science to help them solve it. And in turn, that is I think really the underpinning of taking those frictions away.

人们坐下来思考时，比如说Airbnb，它到底在卖什么？普通人可能会说：“这很明显啊，Airbnb卖的是房间。我去那里预订我想住的房间。”对吧？其他人会说：“Uber卖什么？Uber卖的是乘车服务。当我需要从一个地方到另一个地方时，就会用Uber。”（00:06:10）：从某种意义上说，你没说错。我是说，用户确实可以通过这些平台获得这些服务。但这并不是平台真正在卖的东西。这是一个很重要的区别。平台上有的人在向你出售这些服务。比如Airbnb上的房东在向你出售房源，Uber上的司机在向你出售乘车服务。但Uber和Airbnb实际上是在向你消除某种阻碍——比如找住宿的麻烦，找司机的麻烦。（00:06:42）：在经济学中，我们把这些东西称为交易成本。当你学习经济学入门课时，你会了解市场如何实现供需匹配，并由此得出价格。但直到经济学201课程，你才会明白市场并非总是有效运行。市场不总是有效的原因之一，就是存在各种因摩擦而导致的市场失灵。那么什么是市场失灵呢？比如莱尼想从帕洛阿尔托去伯灵格梅，但却做不到。为什么做不到？因为找不到愿意载他的人。但他为什么不直接打车呢？但该打给谁呢？这些人是谁？他们现在在吗？周五上午10点，他们愿意载他去某个地方吗？（00:07:22）：当我旅行时想找个地方住，面临的摩擦是，谁愿意把房间租给我？原则上，总有人愿意让我住在他们的客厅，但我不知道他们是谁。（00:07:31）：这些都是摩擦，而市场平台向你出售的正是消除这些摩擦。这就是你付钱给他们的原因。这是一个重要的观察，因为这意味着市场的客户不只是购买乘车服务的人，他们还在购买房源。实际上，Airbnb的房东也是客户，Uber的司机也是客户。因此，市场平台的两端都是平台的客户。双方都依赖平台来消除这些摩擦。因为正如你想找个地方住或想打车一样，司机在Uber上是因为想通过载客赚钱，房东在Airbnb上是因为想通过出售房源赚钱。（00:08:10）：我认为，我们通过消除交易成本来赚钱的这个概念，是市场平台领域被误解的一个根本理念。当你作为创业者创办市场平台或思考商业模式时，我认为如果你忘记了这才是你的核心价值主张，就会大错特错。然后你问到数据，以及更广泛的数据科学在市场平台中的作用。（00:08:36）：这很有趣，对吧？我最喜欢举的例子是希腊的古代集市或罗马的图拉真市场。当你看这些地方的图片时，真正让我印象深刻的是石头。我是说，这些地方都是石头做的。如果你想把一个摊位从一个地方搬到另一个地方，就必须先把大量石头从一个地方搬到另一个地方。（00:09:00）：所以你
快进到2023年，如今技术几乎渗透到每一种商业模式中。这意味着我们可以随时调整和重构市场架构，而这正是我们一直在做的事情。（00:09:14）：那些被消除的摩擦点，之所以能被消除，是因为数据和数据科学的支持。所以我想为大家重点强调其中的三个要素，希望大家能将它们视为一个循环。但首先，让我们逐一展开。（00:09:29）：其中之一是寻找匹配的对象。即“我想住在某个地方。谁愿意在特定时间段接待我？”如果我是房东，我有房源。谁愿意在我有空房时入住我的住所？这就是寻找匹配对象的过程。（00:09:49）：接下来是匹配过程。回想我在oDesk的经历，我们当时面临的一个大问题是，如果我有多个求职者申请同一个职位，该选谁？该面试谁？这是现实世界中常见的问题，但现在都是远程操作。我无法亲自见面这些求职者，只能查看他们提交的申请，需要帮助筛选可能的合作伙伴。（00:10:16）：最后是匹配结果反馈。那么匹配结果告诉我们什么呢？比如在Airbnb预订住宿后，你会了解房东和房源信息，房东也会了解你的情况。这所有信息都应该反馈到平台中。因此我们需要评分系统和反馈系统，甚至被动数据收集。比如你提前离开预订地点，可能意味着体验不尽如人意。这就是被动数据收集。你给出五星评价，则是主动数据收集。（00:10:47）：将这些信息反馈回系统后，会带来什么改变？这能让我们更有效地寻找潜在匹配对象，并在未来达成更多匹配。刚才提到的每个环节——寻找潜在匹配对象、促成匹配、了解匹配结果并再次循环——这正是市场数据科学的核心所在。（00:11:05）：我认为每个垂直领域的市场都面临着这三个问题，并依赖数据科学算法来解决它们。反过来，这也正是消除摩擦的核心驱动力。

And there's often these recurring failures of types of marketplaces that just don't work in an area. I was just writing a couple ideas down while you were chatting like cleaners, getting cleaners as a marketplace doesn't seem to work ever. Car wash, there's a classic failure too. Getting tasks done for you on demand as a marketplace seems to not often work. (00:11:46): So this might be too big of a question, but I'm just curious if anything comes up of when someone is starting a marketplace or thinking about starting a marketplace business, what do you find are the most common flaws in, this is probably not going to work as a marketplace?
turns.zh: 许多创业者试图创办市场型企业，却总是在本不存在市场机会的领域寻找机遇。很多这类市场型业务往往屡屡失败，比如在某个地区，清洁工市场就始终难以成功。洗车行业同样是个经典的失败案例。按需为用户完成任务的市场型服务模式似乎也难逃失败的命运。（00:11:46）：这个问题可能太宏大了，但我很好奇，当有人打算创办市场型企业或考虑市场型商业模式时，最常见的缺陷是什么？这种模式很可能无法成功，对吧？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: That is such a fantastic question, and I want to preface what I say with a couple of comments. So one of them is that I've worked with a lot of different marketplace companies, but anything I say is pertaining to something more sensitive. I may not name the company over the course of the podcast. (00:12:17): But the other more important thing I want to say is that I'm a professor at Stanford, and there's a reason I'm not a successful scaled entrepreneur of marketplaces, and that's because I probably haven't unlocked the key to exactly the question you asked. But nevertheless, I have some thoughts on it. (00:12:33): The most important one is this. What I've found talking to people who want to start what they think is a marketplace is that they think too much about a marketplace before they're a marketplace. That in my view is the biggest failure mode. (00:12:46): You mentioned specific things, cleaners. I wonder about that, right? Is it something about the cleaning industry? It possibly is. I don't claim to be an expert on the microeconomics of the cleaning industry. But often it's not that, it's that I thought I was building a marketplace from the beginning, and that's not the way the world works. So I'll give you one vignette of this that I really like, and that's UrbanSitter. (00:13:09): So first, UrbanSitter is a babysitting marketplace. We can talk about their whole life story, but I think what's most interesting is really the early days. And in the early days, what I found interesting, the way I found out about them actually is that we were stuck looking for some help. And I found out about this new platform where the clever thing was when you used to hire a babysitter, it's like pre Venmo days, you needed cash on hand. Because when the babysitter's done at the end of the day, they're usually high school suits or something. They want to get paid. They're not going to take your IOU, that you'll send them some check in the mail the next day. (00:13:43): And unfortunately, you often don't have cash. They don't take credit card. They're high school students. That was an incredible friction to address, which is literally just we accept credit card payments for babysitting. That's it, right? (00:13:55): Now from there, what happened is they took advantage of Facebook networks between parents and babysitters to build trusted introductions. So let's say my sitter wasn't available. I get to know sitters in the Facebook network of that sitter. And once they overcame that first thing to get some liquidity onto their platform, they could move towards asking, how do I solve for these frictions that I talked about earlier? How do I solve for helping people find potential matches? How do I solve for people making those matches, right? You can't do that when you don't have liquidity on your platform. It's silly to tell someone, "Hey, I'm really going to help you find all those drivers out there, even though I only have three drivers on my platform." That's not a friction you're solving for. (00:14:36): So in their example, as they evolved, they actually shifted their monetization model away from billing specifically for this friction of allowing you to pay with credit cards, instead to now billing for how you were interviewing and contacting sitters. They had a two-part plan for that. One with a pay as you go menu, one with a more of a subscription option. But the key thing was either way, what you were paying for now was finding potential babysitters, not paying them with a credit card. That wasn't the key thing anymore. (00:15:05): So what's the moral there? The moral is a marketplace business never starts as a marketplace business, because what we think of as a marketplace business is something which at scale is removing the friction of the two sides finding each other. But when you start, you don't have that scale. (00:15:22): So when you start, you had better be thinking, "What's my value proposition in a world in which I don't have that scaled liquidity on both sides?" And that's bespoke. It means different things. And in the case of oDesk, where I started, that initial thing was that remote work is a weird thing, because basically you've somehow got to know that this person who you're not next to is doing what you're asking them to do. And so the initial value proposition of oDesk was to provide tools for workers to verify they were working the hours and doing the things that they said they were doing, screenshots and various kinds of tracking. (00:16:01): And then in return for that, to be able to provide guarantees on both sides. So now the workers could say, "Hey, I worked what I said so I should get paid." And the employers could say, "I actually see that you worked what you said. And so I feel comfortable that I got what I paid for." That was the initial value proposition, is resolving a trust issue at a remote scale. (00:16:21): At that point, liquidity isn't the game. It's asking, what's a problem that people in this space are facing that I can deal with when I'm not a scaled marketplace? So again, with the cleaning industry, I can comment on that from personal experience, but otherwise, I think that's the way I would think about it. It's almost never about building a marketplace when you're building a marketplace.
turns.zh:
这真是个绝妙的问题，不过在展开讨论前，我想先说几点看法。首先，我曾与众多市场平台公司合作过，但我所谈论的内容可能涉及更敏感的信息，所以在播客中我不会点名具体公司。（00:12:17）另外，我想强调的是，我是斯坦福大学的教授，所以我并非成功的市场平台创业者。这或许是因为我尚未破解你所提问题的关键所在，但我对此还是有一些思考的。（00:12:33）最重要的一点是，我发现许多想创办所谓市场平台的人，在尚未真正成为平台之前就过度纠结于平台的定义。这在我看来是最大的失败模式。（00:12:46）你提到了具体案例，比如清洁工服务。我对此深有体会——这或许与清洁行业的微观经济学有关，但我不敢自诩是该行业的专家。不过通常问题不在于此，而在于我从一开始就试图构建一个完整的市场平台，但现实并非如此。让我分享一个我很喜欢的案例——UrbanSitter。（00:13:09）首先，UrbanSitter是一个保姆市场平台。我们可以聊聊他们的完整发展历程，但最有趣的还是初创阶段。我最初了解到他们的方式，是因为我们当时急需保姆帮助。当时我们发现一个创新点：在Venmo时代之前，雇佣保姆通常需要现金支付。毕竟保姆结束工作后，通常是高中生之类的，他们希望立即获得报酬，而不是等你第二天寄支票。（00:13:43）遗憾的是，现金支付往往不现实。他们不接受信用卡支付，保姆们都是学生。这是一个亟待解决的痛点——直接接受信用卡支付即可。（00:13:55）接下来他们利用Facebook平台上的家长和保姆社交网络，建立信任推荐机制。比如当我的保姆临时有事时，我可以通过她的Facebook好友网找到合适人选。一旦解决了平台流动性问题，才能着手解决前面提到的痛点：如何匹配供需，如何促进用户完成交易。在没有足够用户的情况下，光是告诉别人“我能帮你找到所有司机”是没有意义的。（00:14:36）以UrbanSitter为例，随着业务发展，他们逐渐调整了盈利模式，从收取信用卡支付的手续费转向基于用户面试和联系保姆的收费模式。他们采取了两部分收费策略：一是按次付费，另一是订阅模式。但核心逻辑始终不变——用户付费的重点从信用卡支付转向寻找潜在保姆，这才是关键所在。（00:15:05）
启示是什么？启示是，市场平台型业务绝非一开始就定位为市场平台型业务，因为我们所理解的市场平台型业务，其核心价值在于通过规模化运营消除交易双方的信息不对称。但在创业初期，你根本不具备这样的规模优势。（00:15:22）所以创业伊始，你就必须思考：“在缺乏双方规模化流动性的环境下，我的核心价值主张是什么？” 这需要因地制宜，因人而异。以我创立的oDesk为例，最初的核心价值在于远程工作场景中的信任问题。用户需要确认远程员工是否如约完成了工作任务，于是我们开发了屏幕截图验证、工作时长追踪等工具，并通过这些功能为双方提供信任担保。（00:16:01）当时，市场流动性并非核心难题，关键在于找到一个在缺乏规模化优势的情况下也能解决信任问题的方案。（00:16:21）在这种情况下，创业者不应盲目追随“打造市场平台”的思路，而是要深入思考：当你尚未具备规模化优势时，如何解决目标领域的核心痛点？以清洁服务行业为例，我可以结合个人经验谈谈看法，但总的来说，这才是创业者应有的思维模式——在构建市场平台时，几乎从不从头开始打造市场平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's very similar to the advice I always give marketplace founders, is 90% of your problems are going to be non marketplace specific problems. They're going to be the same problems any startup is going to have. How do I grow? It's going to be the same things you need to do.
turns.zh: 这和我常给市场平台创始人的建议非常相似——你遇到的90%问题都与市场平台无关，而是与任何初创企业都会面临的共性挑战相关。比如：如何实现增长？你需要做的事其实都是大同小异的。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: So one thing you said was, "That's what you tell marketplace founders." I mean, something I've actually pressed hard on in my own way of thinking about this is that maybe we shouldn't talk about the concept of a marketplace founder. Really there's founders. And I think every entrepreneur... I mean one way to think about it, right? It's very hard to think about a human business endeavor that has not been disrupted by the potential for transactions to take place online. (00:17:24): And if that's the case, it means literally any founder is a marketplace founder. It'll be a choice they make after they grow as to whether they want to build a platform. I mean, to take a very hot recent example, no one in their right mind would've thought of OpenAI as a marketplace, but OpenAI is a marketplace now. They may not want to call themselves a marketplace, but they have plugins. The plugins are flooding that platform. People have played with it. It's not an easy thing to find the plugin you need for what you want to do. And that really is a two-sided thing now. There's the plugin creators and there's the users. And they may believe it, they may not believe it, but they are a marketplace. (00:18:04): So I think a different way to think about it is every founder is a marketplace founder. It's going to be a choice they want to make for themselves of whether they want to become that platform. That's I think one. And two is because that's the case, I think one of the other challenges I find founders struggle with is you don't want to overcommit your future. And what I mean by that is that you're building up trust, and you're building up a sense of what kind of business you are in your early days. If you believe that this kind of platform future awaits you, or market platform future awaits you, there may be choices you're making early on that are tying your hands later. (00:18:41): A great example of this is when oDesk started, it was because the tools they were providing were for ongoing monitoring of work. It's a very natural thing to say, "We will just take a constant fraction of the dollars that cross the platform." That all works well and good until after you become mature. Some of these relationships between worker and employer last a long time, and most of the value was generated now not so much because they're able to track each other, because the trust is now there, but because they found each other, because they're able to build that relationship through oDesk. (00:19:16): That meant that the longer that goes on, the less value the platform is adding into that relationship, but you're still pulling 10% of all the dollars. So what does that lead to? A word that most marketplace CEOs know well is disintermediation, which is where you were intermediating between the two parties, and now disintermediation means that essentially they're like, "Hey, we don't need you anymore." (00:19:39): My favorite example is we had some stuff delivered from IKEA by a Thumbtack worker once, and my wife is like, "Oh, thanks a lot. You're so reliable." He's like, "Hey, great. Here's my business card. Ever need me again? Just call the number on the back." And that was it. Thumbtack got their one lead gen, and then we didn't need the platform anymore. (00:19:57): And I think this issue for oDesk meant that after they merged with Elance and became Upwork, they had to think a little bit about, "Okay, what's the monetization strategy we want to use? How do we address this issue that longer term relationships may disintermediate? And does that mean you need a pricing plan that actually takes that into account?" So early commitments in this case to a particular pricing scheme, particular monetization, can really tie your hands as you then realize later you actually are a platform.
turns.zh:
您之前提到过：“这就是你对市场平台创始人说的话。” 我的意思是，在我自己的思考中，我一直强调的一点是，或许我们不应该谈论“市场平台创始人”这个概念。其实本质上就是“创始人”而已。我认为每位创业者……嗯，这么想或许更合适。很难找到一个不受在线交易潜力影响的传统商业模式。（00:17:24）如果真是这样，那就意味着几乎所有创始人都天然是市场平台的缔造者。他们在发展到一定阶段后，可以选择是否要搭建平台。举个近期的热点案例，OpenAI 原本没人会把它视为市场平台，但如今它就是一个市场平台。虽然他们可能不愿自称市场平台，但其实平台上有插件功能，插件如潮水般涌入这个平台。用户已在平台上进行尝试，但要找到适合自己需求的插件并非易事。这其实就是一个双边市场，现在有插件开发者和用户两大群体。用户或许认同这种模式，或许不认同，但OpenAI确实是一个市场平台。（00:18:04）所以我认为另一种思考方式是：每位创始人都是市场平台的缔造者。这将成为他们自主选择的方向——是否要成为那个平台。这是我认为的第一个观点。第二个观点是，基于上述情况，创始人面临的另一个挑战是不要过度锁定未来。我的意思是，在初期阶段，你需要建立信任，明确自己的商业定位。如果你坚信未来会成为市场平台，那么早期做出的某些决策可能会束缚自己的手脚。（00:18:41）oDesk 刚成立时，提供的工具是用于持续监控工作进展的。这很自然地让他们想：“我们只需抽取平台交易额的一定比例作为分成。” 这种模式在平台成熟前运行良好。但随着平台发展，一些雇佣关系长期维系，价值创造不再依赖于追踪彼此行为，而是基于双方通过 oDesk 建立的信任关系。（00:19:16）这意味着平台对这种关系的增值作用逐渐减弱，但你仍能抽取10%的交易分成。那么结果会怎样？大多数市场平台CEO都熟知的一个词是“去中介化”——即你曾在双方之间搭建桥梁，而如今去中介化意味着用户不再需要你了。（00:19:39）我最喜欢的例子是，有次我们通过 Thumbtack 平台请人帮我们从宜家取货，我妻子感激地说：“太感谢你了，真是太靠谱了。” 对方回：“好的，很高兴认识你。如果有需要再联系我，电话在名片背面。”就这样。Thumbtack 获得了一个潜在客户，而我们再也不需要这个平台了。（00:19:57）我认为 oDesk 的这个问题导致他们与 Elance 合并成为 Upwork 后，必须重新思考：“好吧，我们该采用怎样的变现策略？如何应对长期关系可能被去中介化的风险？这是否意味着需要制定定价方案？”
“那实际上有没有考虑到这一点呢？” 在这种情况下，过早地承诺采用特定的定价方案或特定的盈利模式，可能会束缚住你的手脚，因为你可能随后会意识到，自己实际上就是一个平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like this message. It makes me think about Substack actually, which started as just a platform for newsletter writers. And then they're like, "How do we make this more valuable?" Because they take a cut of everyone's revenue. And they've actually invested heavily on helping drive demand to writers, for example, me. And at this point, over 80% of my subscribers come from Substack's network. And so they've built this marketplace element exactly as you're describing, where they just found, "Here's a pain point, writers need more subscribers. How do we help them drive subscribers?" So they figured out all these ways to create demand.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个观点。它让我想起了Substack这个平台。Substack最初只是一个新闻通讯写作者的平台，后来他们开始思考如何提升平台的价值。因为Substack会抽取用户收入分成，所以他们投入大量资源帮助吸引新订阅者，比如我。如今，我超过80%的订阅者都来自Substack的生态系统。他们构建的市场机制正如你所描述的那样——发现了用户痛点，即创作者需要更多订阅者。于是他们想尽办法创造需求。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: That's a really positive story, where they managed to actually expand the frontier of their business by enabling that network. For every one of those, there's unfortunately a lot of negative stories. I mean, one that I think is very painful is how eBay had a lot of challenges with its seller community as it introduced more and more fine-grained sources of fees. (00:21:25): And I think a lot of that, I mean there's many, many treatises at this point written on eBay, and their history, and how they got to the point that they're at. But I think one kind of simple thing I do want people to think about there is that the sellers on eBay who had matured with the platform, who had grown with it, had come to develop certain expectations about what their lives on that platform would look like. And it's understandable, because a lot of these businesses, they had built their livelihood on that platform. That was their entire business. (00:21:56): So when you now reach in and you say, "I'm going to completely change the rules of the game in which your business model operates," from the perspective of those sellers, that's a breaking of a social contract that's been developed over a very long time. So I love the Substack example, because that's like, "Hey, let me amplify our social contract." But I think for every one of those, there's an eBay warning sign that you can trap yourself a little bit.
turns.zh: Substack通过构建社交网络成功拓展了业务边界，这确实是个积极的案例。但遗憾的是，每个成功故事背后都有许多负面教训。比如eBay在引入细化收费机制后，与卖家群体产生了诸多矛盾。（00:21:25）关于eBay的历史，有很多著作分析其兴衰，但我想强调的一点是，平台上的成熟卖家对其商业模式有着深厚的依赖，这份依赖构成了他们的生计。（00:21:56）当平台突然调整规则时，从卖家的角度看，这无异于撕毁长期形成的社会契约。我很欣赏Substack的做法——他们在强化现有规则的基础上拓展了边界。但每当这种创新出现时，eBay式的警示信号总会让人警醒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to close a loop on this really, I think important point, a lot of people listening to this are probably, "I'm a marketplace founder. I'm building a marketplace," are going to hear this and be like, "Oh shit, maybe I need to rethink how I think about what I'm doing." What would be your piece of advice to people like that? Is it focus on the friction point and it may be a marketplace solution, it may be a managed marketplace, it may be you own the supply? Is that the advice, or what would your advice be to someone that's like, "I'm building a marketplace"? How should they reframe their thinking?
turns.zh: 最后总结这个重要观点：许多听众可能正处于市场平台建设阶段，听到这些观点后会反思自己的思路。你会给这些创业者什么建议？是专注于解决痛点，比如市场管理、托管模式，还是完全掌控供应链？这是否是核心建议？对于打造市场平台的人，你会如何重构他们的思维框架？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Let's go back to kind of thinking about this concept of a marketplace of reducing friction. So the litmus test I like to give to someone who claims to me that they're building a marketplace business or they're a marketplace founder is do you have what I would call scaled liquidity on both sides of your platform? What does scaled liquidity mean? (00:23:13): What it means in lay terms... And by the way, I am a data scientist, and I love to think about these quantitatively. But fundamentally, if it doesn't pass the smell test, then you don't have to keep going with the data science. The smell test is scaled liquidity asks, "Do I have a lot of buyers and a lot of sellers on my platform, or do I only have one of these two, or do I have neither?" If you don't have both, you could call yourself whatever you want to call yourself, but at this moment in time, you're not a marketplace. If you have one, congratulations. You've won the game on one side of the market. And now you if you want, you have a choice point. You can lean into growth on the side that you're doing well with. You got a ton of users, ton of buyers? Great. Lean into it, get more buyers. That's one option. There's no shame in not being a marketplace. Scaling a business is scaling a business. If that's the way to do it, do it. (00:24:05): If you decide you want to be a marketplace, then at that moment when you've got a lot of buyers, but not a lot of sellers, or a lot of sellers, but not a lot of buyers, the choice you're facing is, how do I take advantage of having that one side scaled to attract the other side? We can talk more about that, but there's a lot of ways to kind of hack that, to think about how... So to take Uber as an example, they would walk into a new city, and one thing that Uber was commonly known for doing this was back in the days when really Uber Black was the only service is they just hand out coupons for free rides at events, parties, things like that, to take people home. And that was a way of saying, "Hey, we're subsidizing the drivers in the city. That's our scaled side. Now we're going to use that subsidized driver base to attract riders." (00:24:49): So that's like, how do you get that flywheel going? And again, many people have written about how to take liquidity, scaled liquidity on one side, and use it to attract the other side. (00:24:59): If you don't have either side, don't worry about it. Don't worry about being a marketplace. Worry about scaling one side. And in that world, it opens your visibility up completely into the advice of many, many startup advisors. People who have advice not so much about scaling a marketplace, but about scaling a startup. (00:25:22): And I want to say you got to let the ego go at that point. It's fine to articulate to people that your vision of the future is to be a platform or marketplace. As I said, virtually every business is going to have that option at some point in the modern tech enabled economy anyway. So you're not saying something people don't already know when you tell an advisor or an investor that. But I do think you need to be humble enough at the starting point to recognize that there's no sense in talking about a marketplace if you don't have scaling on either side yet.
turns.zh: 让我们回过头来思考降低摩擦的市场平台这一概念。我喜欢给那些声称自己正在打造市场平台业务或自称是市场平台创始人的人提一个测试问题：你们的平台两端是否拥有我所说的「规模化流动性」？什么是「规模化流动性」呢？（00:23:13）：用通俗的话来说……顺便说一句，我是一名数据科学家，我喜欢从量化角度思考这个问题。但从根本上说，如果这个概念经不起推敲，那就没必要继续进行数据分析了。所谓「规模化流动性」的测试问题是：“我的平台上是否有大量买家和卖家？还是只有其中一方，或者两者皆无？”如果两者皆无，你可以随意自称，但当下你还不是一个市场平台。如果你只有其中一方，那恭喜你，你在一侧的市场上已经取得了成功。现在如果你愿意，你可以做出选择：在表现良好的那一侧加大投入，获取更多买家。这是一个选择。没有市场平台的概念也无妨。规模化业务就是规模化业务。如果这就是你的发展路径，那就坚持下去。（00:24:05）：如果你决定要成为一个市场平台，那么当你平台上买家众多但卖家不足，或者卖家众多但买家不足时，你面临的选择是：如何利用一侧的规模化优势来吸引另一侧的用户？我们可以进一步探讨，但有很多方法可以实现这一目标。比如以Uber为例，他们进入新城市时，常见的做法是在活动、派对等场合发放免费乘车券，将人们送回家。这是一种信号：「嘿，我们正在补贴城市里的司机。这是我们规模化的一侧。现在我们要利用这些补贴司机的用户基础来吸引乘客。」（00:24:49）：那么如何让这个良性循环启动呢？许多人已经写过如何利用一侧的流动性（scaled liquidity）来吸引另一侧用户的文章。（00:24:59）：如果两侧都尚未形成规模，那就别纠结于市场平台的概念了。专注于规模化一侧。在这种情况下，你的视野将完全被许多创业顾问的建议所打开。这些顾问提供的建议并非关于如何构建市场平台，而是关于如何发展初创企业。（00:25:22）：我想说，在这个阶段，你必须放下自负。向人们传达你对未来的愿景是打造一个平台或市场平台，这没问题。但正如我所说，在现代科技赋能的经济中，几乎每家企业在某个阶段都会有这样的选择。所以当你向顾问或投资者提及这一点时，他们并不会感到惊讶。但我确实认为，在起步阶段，你需要足够谦逊地认识到，如果两侧尚未形成规模，那就没必要谈论市场平台了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then it becomes a question of a business model, unit economics of, can I build say a DoorDash, not as a marketplace? Can I just hire a bunch of people delivering? Is this even possible in a different route?
turns.zh: 接下来就变成了商业模式和单位经济学的问题：我能否构建一个类似DoorDash的平台，而不是作为一个市场平台？我能否只雇佣一群送货人员？在不同的路径上，这是否可行？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah, that's a great point. One of the things I think that's useful for people to think about here that you're raising, at some level, it's kind of tied up I think with that question of whether I should have employees, or contract or freelance work on one side of the marketplace. (00:26:23): And that's actually a pretty old question in economics. The way we talk about it often is a distinction between a market or a firm. And one of the interesting puzzles in economics, Ronald Coase is a famous economist who thought about this is, "Well, if markets are so efficient, why do we need firms? If markets are efficient at matching labor up with things that need to get done, why would you ever need a firm?" And that's one of the earliest recognitions that transaction costs are a real thing. And that's one of the things that firms are solving for. (00:26:52): And I love what you're saying because what it's recognizing is, "Hey, for your frictions, the best resolution to that might not be to have a marketplace. It might actually be to have very tightly controlled labor." A good example of this actually, Stitch Fix, I think one of the things that's cool about Stitch Fix is the experience that people had early on with stylists at Stitch Fix.
turns.zh:
是的，你提出的观点很棒。我认为人们需要思考的一个问题是，在某种程度上，这与是否应该在市场一端雇佣员工、使用合同工或自由职业者有关。（00:26:23）：这实际上是经济学中一个相当古老的问题。我们常用的说法是区分市场和企业。经济学家罗纳德·科斯对此的思考很有意思，他提问道："既然市场如此高效，为什么我们还需要企业？如果市场能高效地将劳动力与需求匹配，为什么还要企业？"这就是对交易成本是真实存在这一点的早期认识，也是企业存在的意义之一。
（00:26:52）：我很欣赏你的观点，因为它指出了："对于你的摩擦问题，解决方案可能不是建立市场，而是进行严格的人力资源管控。"一个很好的例子是Stitch Fix，我认为Stitch Fix的亮点之一，就是早期用户与其造型师建立的深度互动体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm a happy customer, by the way. I think [inaudible 00:27:16].
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我是Stitch Fix的忠实用户。我觉得[00:27:16，听不清]。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah, I think one of the great things about that experience is it felt magical to have someone who kind of got to know you. But that depends on a relationship that doesn't feel like a freelance relationship every single time you're going back. (00:27:31): Another example that I would pull out is pretty much any healthcare platform. So for example, for physical therapy, it'd be weird if every time you went to a physical therapy platform, you just got randomly matched to whoever happened to be available then. So I think there's some curation that needs to happen of that relationship. Does that mean full employee? Maybe not. But it does mean you have to think a little bit about exactly as you brought up, what's the nature of curation of your labor pool?
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这种体验的妙处在于，有一个真正了解你的顾问，这感觉很神奇。但这依赖于一种并非每次都像自由职业关系的长期信任关系。（00:27:31）：另一个例子是几乎所有医疗平台。比如物理治疗平台，如果每次去平台都随机匹配到当时刚好有空的医生，那就太奇怪了。所以我认为这种关系需要精心管理。这是否意味着要转为全职员工？或许不必。但这确实意味着你需要像你提到的这样，认真思考如何精心管理你的劳动力资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so let's come back to a point you made early on around the importance of data and the power of data in actually making your marketplace a lot more efficient and work more effectively. So say that you have a data scientist, or a data analyst, or someone that is helping you optimize your marketplace. Where do you often find the biggest leverage and opportunity for a data person to help you make your marketplace more effective?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，回到你早前提到的数据的重要性，以及数据在提升市场效率和效果方面的作用。假设你有一位数据科学家、数据分析师或其他帮助你优化市场的专业人员。数据人员在哪里能找到最大的杠杆作用和机会，帮助你提升市场的效率？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: This is an incredible question, right? Because I think I could answer it a number of different ways. One question I think that's kind of basic, it's just what should this person be doing? And I'm going to actually evade that question a little bit. I'm going to give some examples of what they could do, but I feel like that's one where context matters a lot. (00:28:45): So as an example, at ride-sharing or grocery delivery marketplaces, pricing means actually, what do you pay for that ride? Or what do you pay for that delivery? So that's actually the price that's set at the moment you actually place the order. Just to be clear, by the way, if you order from DoorDash, I don't mean the price of the restaurant. I mean, what do you pay to DoorDash, right? What's that fee? Is there a surcharge, because it's surge or whatever? Okay, so that's a thing, right? (00:29:11): But that's not really a thing in a marketplace where the platform's not setting the prices. So in Airbnb, really hosts are the ones who are in charge of setting prices for their listings. (00:29:21): One answer to your question is, if I'm in a place like Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, I want to have good data scientists thinking about pricing. Because that seems like something which should be heavily dependent on the instantaneous state of supply and demand in my marketplace. So that's one type of answer is, well do I need data scientists working on pricing? Do I need data scientists working on search? Why search? Because maybe in my marketplace, finding the needle in the haystack is really the biggest, highest friction problem. So maybe I need a lot more data scientists saying about search. (00:29:51): That's what I'm going to evade. Okay? I'm going to focus more on something completely different, which is just a more philosophical point about what a data scientist does. (00:30:00): So in a lot of companies today, especially, a main thing that you ask data scientists to do is build what's called a machine learning model. Now, machine learning model even already can mean a lot of things to a lot of different people. I'm going to focus on something very concrete. You're asking them to predict something. (00:30:16): When I started at oDesk, this is in 2012, one of the funny things about me is I started at oDesk because I'd had a academic career up to that point in about 10 years, just building mathematical models of things. I was not really very much of a data scientist up to that point. What I expected would happen is I'd go to industry and I'd be told, "Hey, look how important data is." And definitely my eyes were opened. (00:30:40): And one of the first things I was asked to think about is, well, okay, someone comes to oDesk, post a job, workers apply to that job. Predict which of these workers is most likely to be hired on that job. That was the narrow question. And so why is that a good question? Because we have a whole awesome set of tools now to solve that kind of a problem exactly. How do we do it? Take a lot of past data of past jobs, past applicants, past hires that were made. Then we ask these crazy big black box algorithms, "All right, do the best job you can predicting who's going to get hired on this job with these applicants." And we use that data to test how well these algorithms are doing. That's machine learning in 30 seconds basically. So we're working on this problem. Great. (00:31:25): And then I kind of poked my head up a little bit. I go, "Why are we working? What is this going to do?" Well, it turns out the reason these kinds of things are important is they get used to make decisions. So what kind of decision do you make with that? Well, one thing you do is you say, "Well, if I could predict who's most likely to be hired, then I should just rank people based on that, and that would be a good matching algorithm. That'd be a good way to sort and triage applicants for employers when they're screening, trying to figure out who to interview, who to hire." Great. Sounds pretty natural. (00:31:58): And then you think about it a little bit, and this to me, it's such a passion project to get people to understand that this is why the humans in the loop that help us in businesses and making sense of data are so critical, is the following problem. (00:32:15): If you think about it a little bit, you realize what that algorithm is doing, it's really just picking up on patterns in past data. So yeah, that's great. This person is likely to be hired. But what we really want is something different. We're trying to add value by ranking people. (00:32:32): So to give another example that's similar to this, when you're a marketing manager, and you've got a cracked data science team that's built a long-term value, lifetime value model for you, you're not going to get in trouble with anyone if you send your highest value promotions to the highest LTV customers, right? Who's going to blame you for that? Because you're like, "This person is worth a lot, and I sent them this promotion." Say that in your monthly report, nobody's going to give you a hard time. (00:32:59): But the problem with that way of thinking is actually predicting what their lifetime value is isn't really the question. The question is, how much more are they going to spend on my platform because I sent them that promotion? (00:33:11): That's a very different thing. It's a differential rather than an absolute. I'm not interested in their absolute LTV. I'm absolutely interested in the difference in their LTV because I sent them this promotion. (00:33:21): And when you look at it that way, what you realize can happen is picking up on patterns because of good predictions, right? Finding the people that have high LTV because you predicted that is very different than making good decisions, which is about saying the difference in their LTV is going to be higher because I sent them this promotion. (00:33:39): I love this example, because I taught a class here at Stanford. It was like an executive education class. We had all the executives from a company in the room, and one of the people in the room was the chief marketing officer. And I just asked this question like, "Hey, okay, let's say you got this great LTV model, who would you send the promotions to?" It's like, "Definitely the highest LTV people," and there's a CMO in the room. And so it's a little bit of a delicate situation, like pushing back a little bit, right? (00:34:03): I do want to be clear, there's reputational reasons you might do that anyway. I mean, I'm not trying to get away from that. But just to make the narrow point that predicting is about picking up patterns, but making decisions, it's about thinking about these differences. (00:34:15): Now, why is that important? Because we learn in high school, correlation is not causation. That's a phrase everybody has heard all over the place. What does that have to do with this? Well, when we teach people to build machine learning models, we're asking them to make predictions, we're asking them to find correlations. Prediction is inherently about correlation. But when we ask people to make decisions, we're asking them to think about causation. "If I make this decision, then will I actually increase the net value of my business? Will I have by sending the promotion, increased the likelihood that this person is going to spend more on my platform?" (00:34:50): And so the first and most important thing that I feel very strongly about in what would I get a data scientist to do is no matter who they are, even if it was that person in the weeds thinking about building this prediction model for hiring, get them to be thinking in the back of their mind always that their goal is to help the business make decisions. And that the distinction between causation and correlation matters a lot. We can talk a lot more about how does that play out in terms of their day-to-day work. But at least at a starting point, you have to recognize that the first step is always recognition that prediction isn't the same thing as making decisions.
turns.zh:
这真是个很棒的问题，对吧？因为我觉得我可以用多种方式来回答它。首先，我认为一个最基本的问题是——这个人应该做什么？不过我暂时先回避这个问题。我会举几个例子，说明他们可以做些什么，但我觉得这个问题很大程度上取决于上下文。（00:28:45）比如，在拼车或食品配送平台上，定价其实指的是用户实际支付的费用。也就是说，当你下单时，价格就是即时确定的。顺便说一句，如果你通过DoorDash下单，我指的不是餐厅的价格，而是你向DoorDash支付的费用，对吧？这笔费用有附加费吗？比如高峰时段加价之类的？好的，这就是一个例子。（00:29:11）但在不由平台设定价格的市场中，这就不是问题了。比如在Airbnb上，房东负责为自己的房源定价。（00:29:21）对于你的问题，我的回答是，如果我在Uber、Lyft或DoorDash这样的平台工作，我希望有优秀的数据科学家来研究定价策略。因为这似乎应该高度依赖于市场上供需的即时状态。所以一个可能的答案是——我们需要数据科学家研究定价吗？还是需要他们专注于搜索？为什么是搜索？因为在我的市场中，“大海捞针”可能是最大的、最费力的难题。所以或许我需要更多数据科学家专注于搜索。（00:29:51）这就是我要回避的问题。好的，我会转向一个完全不同的话题——关于数据科学家职责的更哲学层面的思考。（00:30:00）如今许多公司，特别是大型公司，让数据科学家做的最主要的工作就是构建所谓的机器学习模型。现在，机器学习模型对不同的人可能意味着不同的东西。我将重点谈论一个非常具体的应用场景——预测某个结果。（00:30:16）2012年我加入oDesk时，最有趣的事情之一是，我从学术界转行到工业界，因为在那之前的十年里，我一直在构建数学模型。那时我还算不上真正的数据科学家。当时我预期自己进入行业后，会被告知“数据有多重要”。确实让我大开眼界。（00:30:40）我被要求思考的第一个问题是——好吧，有人来到oDesk，发布一个职位空缺，求职者申请该职位。我们要预测哪个求职者最有可能被录用。这个问题很具体。那么为什么这是个好问题？因为我们现在有一套强大的工具来准确解决这类问题。如何实现？收集过去的职位数据、申请者数据和招聘记录。然后让那些复杂的黑盒算法尽可能准确地预测哪些申请者最有可能被录用。我们用这些数据来测试算法的效果。这就是30秒速成版的机器学习。接着我们开始着手解决这个问题。很棒。（00:31:25）然后我稍微探头看看。我问：“我们为什么要做这个？这有什么用？”结果发现，这类事情之所以重要，是因为它们能
用于做决策。那么你会用它来做什么样的决策呢？嗯，你可以这么想："如果我能预测谁最有可能被录用，那我就应该根据这个预测对人们进行排序，这会是一个很好的匹配算法。当雇主筛选求职者、决定面试谁、录用谁时，用这个算法来分类和筛选求职者会很有效。"听起来挺自然的。（00:31:58）但你再仔细想想，对我来说，这个问题之所以值得深入探讨，是因为要让人们明白，在商业场景中借助人类参与来理解数据的复杂性是何等重要。（00:32:15）如果你仔细思考一下，就会发现这个算法实际上只是在识别过去数据中的模式。这固然不错，但我们真正需要的是另一种价值创造——通过排序来提升决策质量。（00:32:32）再举个类似的例子：当你是一名营销经理，手下有一个数据科学团队为你构建了长期价值（LTV）模型时，如果你把最高价值的促销活动发送给LTV最高的客户，应该没人会责怪你吧？因为你可以说：“这个人价值很高，我给他发了促销活动。”把这写进月报里，没人会找你麻烦。（00:32:59）但这种思维方式的问题在于，预测他们的LTV值并非关键问题。关键问题是，因为发送了促销活动，他们在我的平台上会多花多少钱？（00:33:11）这完全是两个不同的概念。前者是相对差异，后者是绝对值。我对他们的绝对LTV不感兴趣，我只对发送促销活动后LTV的增量感兴趣。（00:33:21）这样看，你会发现预测模式和做出决策是两回事。预测出LTV高的人，并不等于做出决策——即预测发送促销活动后LTV的增量才是关键。（00:33:39）我特别喜欢这个例子，因为我在斯坦福大学教过一门课。这是一门高管教育课程，教室里坐满了公司高管，其中一位是首席营销官。当我问这个问题时，大家都回答：“肯定是LTV最高的用户啊。”但首席营销官也在场，所以场面有点微妙，需要稍微委婉地反驳。（00:34:03）我必须说明，出于声誉考量，你可能还是会这么做。我不是想回避这个问题，只是想强调预测是识别模式，而决策是思考差异。（00:34:15）那么为什么这很重要呢？因为我们在高中就学过，相关性不等于因果关系。这是句老生常谈的名言。但这和我们的问题有什么关系呢？当我们教人们构建机器学习模型时，我们要求他们做预测，寻找相关性。预测本质上就是相关性。但当我们让人们做决策时，我们要求他们思考这些差异。
因果关系。“如果我做出这个决定，那么我的业务净值是否真的会增加？通过发送促销信息，是否会提高这名用户在我的平台上消费的可能性？”（00:34:50）  
因此，在我看来，让数据科学家做的最重要的一件事——无论他们是谁，即便只是那个正为招聘而构建预测模型的初级人员——都要让他们始终牢记，自己的目标是帮助企业做出决策。因果关系和相关性的区别至关重要。我们可以深入探讨这在日常工作中的具体体现，但至少在起点阶段，你必须认识到，预测与决策本质不同，这才是第一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the takeaway here is as a data team and as a data scientist on the team, is help the business make predictions. Are there a couple more examples you could share of just what is an example of a decision that you think they often should be making and using data to help them with?
turns.zh: 因此，关键要点是，作为数据团队和团队中的数据科学家，我们的核心任务是帮助企业进行预测。您能否再举几个例子，说明您认为企业在何种情况下应当利用数据来辅助决策？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Maybe the right frame of reference for this, and the word that an academic would use is causal inference. So what we're changing from is machine learning to causal inference. So let's think that through in a couple of different use cases that are related to that marketplace data science flywheel I talked about earlier. Finding matches, making matches, and then learning about matches. (00:36:04): So finding matches, like you said, a core part of that is search and recommendation, and each of those relies on rankings. So I want to be able to rank order. Let's say I go do a search on Airbnb. On a rank order, the different listings in the marketplace, right? At some level, it's true that what I'm trying to do there is I'm trying to just predict, what are you going to like the most? (00:36:24): But I think there's an important piece of that also, which is that I want to think a little bit about the distinction between two different ranking algorithms. That's the real decision that's being made. (00:36:35): And when I think about the distinction between two different ranking algorithms, I don't want to be only comparing them in terms of how well they recreate the choices people made in the past. The way I'm really going to evaluate those is in my market, does one of those lead to better matches or more matches than the other one, right? (00:36:54): So Airbnb as a business, what are the most obvious core metrics? It's bookings and revenue. So you're going to want to ask a very basic question. If I use the ranking algorithm Lenny just developed last night versus the ranking algorithm Ramesh developed last week, does Lenny's ranking algorithm lead to more bookings than Ramesh's ranking algorithm? (00:37:11): And it's so important to put it that way starkly, because that's so different a question than, does Lenny's ranking algorithm do a better job of predicting over the last two years what bookings people made than Ramesh's ranking algorithm? So that's I think at that level. (00:37:24): Then we talked a little bit about ranking at the point of making a match, and I think that's where this hiring issue popped up. Because in the end, while we might have these predictive algorithms to rank who you're going to hire, that's not the important question. (00:37:38): Interestingly, the important question is actually to evaluate the quality of the match that's made. And we would do that through the next step of that flywheel. We'd ask ourselves, what ratings did they give back to that freelancer? Do they hire that freelancer again? So you're comparing two different algorithms not through their ability to recreate the past, but their ability to make matches in the future that can be objectively evaluated to say, "Hey, I increased the value of the business. I actually made better matches this way." And then rating systems, I think we could talk quite a bit about a similar phenomenon there too.
turns.zh: 或许这方面的参考框架，或者说学术界常用的术语，叫做因果推断。所以我们要从机器学习转向因果推断。接下来，我想通过几个与我之前提到的市场数据科学飞轮相关的用例来探讨这一点。首先是寻找匹配、建立匹配，然后从匹配中获取洞察。（00:36:04）：寻找匹配，正如您所说，核心在于搜索和推荐，而这两者都依赖于排名。例如，我在Airbnb上进行搜索时，平台会对不同房源进行排名，对吧？从某种程度上说，我试图预测用户最可能喜欢的房源，这确实是一种预测行为。（00:36:24）：但我认为还有一个重要点，那就是我需要区分两种不同的排名算法。这才是真正的决策。（00:36:35）：当我区分两种不同的排名算法时，我不想仅从它们重现过去用户选择的准确性来评估它们。我真正要评估的是，在我的市场中，哪种算法能带来比另一种更好的匹配或更多匹配？（00:36:54）：那么，Airbnb作为一家企业，最明显的核心指标是什么？是预订量和收入。因此，您会想问一个非常基础的问题：如果我使用Lenny昨晚开发的排名算法，而非Ramesh上周开发的算法，Lenny的算法是否能带来比Ramesh的算法更多的预订量？（00:37:11）：这种表述方式至关重要，因为这与“Lenny的排名算法在过去两年中是否比Ramesh的算法更好地预测了用户的预订行为？”这样的问题截然不同。（00:37:24）：接下来我们谈到了匹配阶段的排名问题，而招聘问题也正是在此处浮出水面的。因为最终，虽然我们可能有这些预测算法来对用户进行排名，但这并非关键问题。（00:37:38）有趣的是，关键问题实际上在于评估匹配的质量。我们会通过飞轮的下一步来实现这一目标。我们会自问，用户给那位自由职业者打了什么评分？他们会再次雇用那位自由职业者吗？因此，我们对两种算法的评估不应基于它们重现过去的能力，而应基于它们在未来建立匹配的能力，而这种匹配能力可以通过客观评估来证明：“嘿，我提升了企业的价值。用这种方式匹配效果更好。”至于评分系统，我认为我们也可以对其中的类似现象进行深入探讨。
