turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah. First of all, I'm really glad you broached the E word. I was dancing around it, and I'm really glad that we talked about experiments. Because yeah, one of the big lessons of this recent conversation we've been having is just, how could you possibly know that difference without doing something like experimenting? (00:40:38): So yeah, I am a big believer in experiments. I mean, I'll just lay those cards on the table. I love working with businesses that think experiments are important to helping make good decisions. (00:40:49): Now all that said, I am also someone who feels pretty strongly about this exact issue that you're raising. It's just, you can't experiment your way out of everything. (00:40:57): And one frame I like to give people is that although you might say you're an experiment driven business, some businesses will proclaim, "We literally test everything." What that kind of leaves aside a little bit is there's a lot of degrees of freedom in what it means to test everything. (00:41:15): Because ultimately, what's getting built and tested are choices that are made through the organizational structure, the data scientists, the PMs, the engineers, everybody's on... Before we're running experiments, we're actually thinking about even what's worth experimenting, what designs are we coming with? So that's one. (00:41:33): And the other big one is, how long do we run these experiments? Okay, that's a big choice. And what I generally believe, and I think there's a paper we can link to later that I'll point your readers to as well that... Not my paper, from some folks at Microsoft. (00:41:49): What I generally believe is we're risk averse on both these two dimensions, that what people decide to test in a world that has promoted experimentation for everything tends to be more incremental by design. Okay? And we'll come back to that actually, answer the because in a second. So that's one. And two is people tend to run experiments for a long time, and probably longer than they should. (00:42:14): Now, what do I mean by these two things? So what's interesting to me about this dynamic is experiments don't live in a vacuum. Companies have incentives. And in companies that really go all in on experimentation, one of the things that gets wrapped up in that is the incentives around experiments. Because if you go all in on experiments, a common thing you'll see is data scientists get judged based on how many wins they had that quarter. How do you get more wins? (00:42:43): Well, it's easier to get wins when you're being incremental. And because it's important to have wins, you have to run them long enough to demonstrate that they're really wins. You're less willing to cut something off in exchange for trying something riskier. (00:42:56): So the big lesson of this Microsoft paper, it's called A/B Testing with what's called Fat Tails, which in lay terms just means you're running a business where there's potentially big opportunities out there if you look at the effects of the experiments that you run. There's a couple of lessons there about both trying a lot more stuff that's not all risk averse, and not necessarily running everything for so long. So really getting velocity up. (00:43:20): So you could see that there's a big incentive problem there, because the culture that says it's okay to fail big actually requires changing the terminology of wins. This is one of the things I hate most in A/B testing, I have to say. I get where it comes from. Experimentation was never historically in science about winners and losers. It'd be weird if it Ronald Fisher who's kind of the father of experimentation with his agriculture experiments talked about winners. I don't think that's necessarily how he talked about things. Experimentation is always very hypothesis driven. It's about, what are you learning? (00:43:53): And that's really an important distinction because what it means is if I go with something big, risky, and it, "fails," meaning that doesn't win. Nevertheless, if I was being rigorous about what hypotheses that's testing about my business, I'm potentially learning a lot. (00:44:11): So a great example of this kind of thing is that there's an important feature of marketplaces is badging. So sometimes, it's really important to have badges on your top-rated profiles or whatever, when people are searching. (00:44:26): And without going too far into the details, a common finding with badges is that badges you think are going to be great actually turn out to be terrible. And one reason they're terrible is they focus too much attention on the badged folks, and pull too much attention away from the unbadged folks. (00:44:44): And if we judge that only in terms of winners and losers, you throw the baby out with the bath water, you're like, "Well that badging idea was terrible. So ditch that, no badges." (00:44:51): But that's not what it's telling you. It's teaching you something about how inventory is being reallocated, how attention's being redirected through the badges. And you really want to think not in terms of winning and losing, but learning. (00:45:05): So learning is a win. And I feel that that's a cultural thing fundamentally. It's very hard to somehow attach dollars and cents at the top to data scientists running experiments that fail, but learn. And ultimately, I think getting into that space where you experiment more, meaning you don't run all your experiments for quite as long and you accept the willingness to try experiments that are into the tails where you might fail bigger is a cultural thing. It's about saying that, "We're allowing that to be part of our social contract with our data scientists," or actually our employee contract with our data scientists, that not everything is just about how many launches you had and how many wins there were. (00:45:45): It's okay to say, "That's how I want to use experimentation," but if you're going to use it that way, then I would say don't be a, "We experiment everything," business. Because then I think you need some other way to deal with these big changes that teach the whole company a lot, but maybe can't fall into the incentives you've created for your data scientists.
turns.zh:
是啊首先，我真的很高兴你提到了“实验”这个词。我之前一直避而不谈，但很高兴我们今天能聊聊实验这件事。因为没错，最近我们讨论的一个重要经验就是：如果不通过实验来验证差异，你怎么可能真正理解其中的不同呢？（00:40:38）所以我确实非常推崇实验。说实话，我得把话说清楚。我喜欢和那些认为实验对决策至关重要的企业合作。（00:40:49）不过说了这么多，我对你们提到的这个问题也深有体会。毕竟，不是所有问题都能靠实验来解决。（00:40:57）我常给人的建议是，虽然有些公司自诩“以实验为导向”，但他们往往宣称“我们什么都测试”。但这忽略了一个关键点：测试的自由度其实有很多层级。（00:41:15）因为最终，决定要测试的内容，往往是组织架构、数据科学家、产品经理、工程师等多方共同协作的结果。在开展实验之前，我们首先要思考：哪些问题值得测试？哪些设计方案值得探索？这就是第一层。（00:41:33）第二个关键点是，实验的持续时间往往过长。这是个很重要的决策。我认为微软团队的一篇论文（不是我写的）能很好地说明这个问题：当整个行业都在推崇实验时，人们往往倾向于进行渐进式测试。（00:42:14）那么这两个问题具体指什么呢？让我来解释一下背后的逻辑。实验并非孤立存在，企业有其内在激励机制。在那些全力推行实验的公司里，围绕实验的激励体系至关重要。比如，数据科学家往往会根据季度内的“成功案例”来评判绩效。但如何才能获得更多成功案例呢？（00:42:43）渐进式测试更容易取得成功，而为了证明成功，需要让实验持续足够久。人们往往不愿中止实验，宁愿冒险尝试新方案。（00:42:56）微软那篇论文提到的A/B测试中的“厚尾效应”概念很值得玩味。简单来说，就是当你测试的项目可能带来巨大回报时，就需要用更长的时间来验证其价值。这启发我们要勇于尝试更多非渐进式实验，同时避免过度延长实验周期。真正提升实验效率的关键在于，改变对失败的定义文化。说实话，这是我最反感A/B测试的地方。但我理解其背后的逻辑——实验在科学领域本质上不是非黑即白的，追求失败的文化本质上是反人性的。
罗纳德·费舍尔（Ronald Fisher）——农业实验之父——曾谈及“赢家”与“输家”。但我认为他对此的理解未必如此。实验始终是以假设为导向的。关键在于：你能从中收获什么？（00:43:53）  
这是一个重要的区分，因为这意味着即便某项大胆的尝试以失败告终（即未能成为“赢家”），只要我能严格审视背后的商业假设，就能从中汲取宝贵经验。（00:44:11）  
举个典型例子：市场平台的一项重要功能是徽章系统。例如，在搜索页面展示高评分用户的徽章，对用户体验至关重要。（00:44:26）  
但研究发现，看似完美的徽章机制往往适得其反。原因在于，徽章过度聚焦获奖者，反而分散了对普通用户的关注。（00:44:44）  
若仅以成败论英雄，往往因噎废食——认为徽章理念失败后就彻底否定它。（00:44:51）  
但其核心价值在于揭示资源重新分配的规律，以及徽章如何通过注意力偏向重塑生态。（00:45:05）  
学习本身就是胜利。这种文化转变至关重要：数据科学家不应因实验失败而被苛责，而应将失败视为学习的机会。（00:45:45）  
最终，关键在于培养实验文化——允许数据科学家尝试高风险项目，接受失败的成本。（00:45:45）

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This badging example is, I don't know if you're referring to the Airbnb example, but I actually led the launch of Superhost at Airbnb, which is the ultimate badge on Airbnb. And there was a lot of concern from the data team that it would destroy the marketplace, because they've built, as you've described, this very well-crafted ranking algorithm, with just a prediction of exactly as you described, which listings that guest is most likely to book and be successful booking. And then we're about to throw a badge on random listings in the results. And so this one data scientist on our team's like, "No, we can't do this. This is insane. We're going to destroy it all." (00:46:42): And we still went ahead with it. We ran an experiment showing the badge to some people and some not, actually, it was no impact at all. Which Superhost itself had no impact at all on the business as far as we could tell initially, which is also bittersweet because it felt like, "Why did we even work on this thing?" There was a slight benefit where a host felt better, they felt more satisfied with being a host, but I went exactly through what you described, so that's pretty funny.
turns.zh: 关于徽章这个例子，我不知道你是否指的是Airbnb的案例，但我确实曾负责Airbnb超级房东（Superhost）项目的上线工作。这是Airbnb上最顶级的徽章。数据团队当时非常担心，认为引入徽章会破坏平台生态，因为他们精心打造了排名算法，能精准预测用户最可能预订成功的房源。然而我们却要在搜索结果中随机给部分房源添加徽章。团队里有个数据科学家坚决反对：“不行，这样太疯狂了，会毁了整个系统！”（00:46:42）但我们还是推进了这个项目。经过实验，显示徽章的用户和不显示徽章的用户搜索结果没有任何差异。最初看来，Superhost徽章对业务毫无影响，这真是令人又喜又忧——我们不禁自问：“我们当初为什么要做这个项目？” 不过倒是带来了一个微弱的积极影响：房东们对自己的身份认同感更强了，对房东身份的满意度也提升了。但整个过程确实和你描述的如出一辙，真是件趣事。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Without necessarily going into the weeds on the data science of Superhost, I think there's a lot wrapped up in what you said. I guess another thing I'll say is that I'm a big believer that you don't throw your understanding of the business out the window when you process experiment results. And it's partly, I guess what I mean by this is data science is really about accumulation of evidence. It's never about one finding in isolation. And so another kind of trap I think is to sometimes say, "Well, I hit stat sig on my A/B test, green light. It's all go." (00:47:47): And I think you had Ronny Kohavi on your show, and he made a similar point that there are different levels of evidence, and just having an outlier A/B test that goes against everything you believe about your business doesn't mean that you somehow have controverted all your knowledge. And I think that's one side of it. (00:48:05): The other thing is you can't always measure everything that's important that's needed to really develop a full sense. So with Superhost, one of the things that's hard to measure is the long-term impact of Superhost. Because in the short run, Superhost causes a rebalancing of inventory. There's going to be winners and losers. Part of Superhost is actually about retaining hosts that get the badge over a longer period of time. Recognizing that hypothesis actually says something about maybe how long the experiment needs to be run or what kinds of data analyses need to be done. (00:48:38): And in the end, if you can't do that, you can't run it long enough, or you can't do that data analysis due to sparsity of data or lack of data to address the question, it matters what you bring to the table. What are your beliefs about that? (00:48:51): So what I like to tell people to do there is I like to push people to be what's called quantified rather than data-driven, which is, okay fine, some things we can't measure. But maybe you've got a leadership team with different beliefs about what they think the retention value of Superhost is going to be, and they might be all over the place. (00:49:10): You can process your experiment results in the context of these competing beliefs. It's almost like a prediction market kind of a thing. And start asking, "Well okay, if this is what we believe about our business, this is what the data is telling us out of the experiment, let's put those two together and ask, is this enough for us to make the bet that we're still going to go with it?" Even though maybe that short-term test you ran was flat.
turns.zh:
无需深入探讨Superhost的数据科学，我认为你所说的内容中蕴含着诸多深意。另外，我想说的是，在处理实验结果时，你不应将对业务的理解抛诸脑后。数据科学本质上是证据的积累，绝非孤立的某个发现。有些人会想：“我的A/B测试结果达到了统计显著性标准，就可以全速推进了。” （00:47:47）  
我记得你曾邀请Ronny Kohavi做客节目，他也提到过类似观点，即证据有不同的层次。一次异常的A/B测试结果与你对业务的认知相悖，并不意味着你就推翻了所有既有认知。这只是问题的一个方面。  
（00:48:05）  
另一方面，很多对全面理解至关重要的事物并不能被量化。以Superhost为例，长期影响是难以衡量的。短期内，Superhost会导致库存资源重新分配，必然会产生赢家和输家。而Superhost的核心价值在于长期留住获得徽章的房东。这一假设能否成立，取决于实验周期是否足够长、数据分析是否到位，以及数据的稀疏程度或是否足以支撑假设。  
（00:48:38）  
若无法完成这些环节，无法延长实验周期，或因数据稀疏无法进行分析，那么你必须具备批判性思维。面对这些挑战，你的信念有多坚定？  
（00:48:51）  
对此我的建议是，要从量化思维而非数据驱动思维出发。有些问题无法量化，但或许你的领导团队对Superhost的留存价值存在不同假设，这些分歧需要在实验结果中体现。这就像预测市场机制，基于不同假设对实验结果进行验证，进而判断是否值得继续推进。即便短期测试结果平平，也要保持信心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's actually exactly how I think of Superhost looking back. It was a great idea. I'm really happy. I can't even imagine Airbnb without that, even though there's no evidence, at least initially, that it made any impact. I'm guessing they looked at it again, and maybe there's something that came out of it. But even if it had no impact, it just feels like it made the marketplace better. And that was a big learning for me. It doesn't need to always drive a metric that you can measure. There's just like, this is the way it should work.
turns.zh: 回顾Superhost，我认为这正是它的精髓所在。这是个伟大的创意，我为此深感欣慰。即使最初没有证据表明它产生了实际影响，我也无法想象Airbnb没有它会怎样。我猜他们后来重新评估了数据，或许从中获得了启发。但即便没有立竿见影的效果，它至少让市场环境更完善了。这对我来说是个重要启示。数据科学不必总是驱动可量化的指标，它更应遵循事物应然的运行逻辑。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: So one of the reasons the thing you said happens is because marketplaces are a little bit like a game of whac-a-mole, okay? And what I mean by that is, so narrowly in the context of Superhost, because you're redirecting attention to some hosts at the expense of... It's not even obvious if bookings can really go up. Maybe you get lucky and maybe you get a bunch more bookings. One reason you probably wouldn't expect that in the first place is there's only a limited number of Superhosts. How many more bookings are they going to be absorbing because of all this extra attention? And you're taking attention away from other people. Without doing any data analysis, my prior would've been that booking should probably go down. (00:50:33): And one example that I came across with one of the companies I worked with that I love is we were working together over a period of time, and in a month, we looked at some of the data and it suggested that our new supply side was having a pretty bad experience. Say, "We got to do something about this." (00:50:55): So what we decided to do is build some custom bespoke features that were really going to direct them to more experienced folks on the other side of the market. Good. And then lo and behold, pretty soon those metrics start to look better. But then we're looking at it, we're like, "Wait a second. Now the existing folks on the other side are having a worse experience." (00:51:12): So you kind of whiplash around. You're like, "Wait a second, we better do something about that." So we take them, we try to match them up with the more experienced folks. And now suddenly a month after that you're like, "Wait a second." And your metrics just keep moving around. (00:51:24): And that's because the whac-a-mole game here is ultimately, a lot of marketplace management is moving attention and inventory around. Sometimes you get lucky and you really expand the pie for everybody. But I think Servaes Tholen, who was CFO at Upwork that I got to know there and then went to Thumbtack later, he had this line when he came to visit our class that I love, which is, "You have to recognize when you run marketplaces that many of the changes that are most consequential create winners and losers. And rolling with those changes is about recognizing whether the winners you've created are more important to your business view than the losers you've created in the process." And it's a hard reality, because nobody likes to articulate the idea that a feature change is hurting some of the people in your marketplace. But because of this fundamental constraint baked into how marketplaces work, many of the things that we would choose to do and the reallocation they create can't necessarily create observed high expanding wins in the short run. You're often making bets that that's where you're headed, partly through the reallocation that you're doing right now. (00:52:30): And so I think that's interesting about Superhost to me is that partly points to thinking about, what's the objective you would've defined, the metric you would've defined in the short run that captures this idea of a trade-off?
turns.zh: 因此，你提到的这种现象之所以会发生，是因为市场平台有点像玩"打地鼠"的游戏。我的意思是，在Superhost的语境下，由于你将注意力转移到某些房东身上，而牺牲了其他房东的利益……实际上，预订量是否真的会增加尚不明确。也许你运气好能获得更多预订。但你可能首先不会预料到这一点，因为Superhost的数量毕竟有限。那么，额外的关注能让他们多吸收多少预订量呢？而你正从其他人那里夺走注意力。即使不进行数据分析，我原本也会认为预订量应该会下降。（00:50:33）：我曾遇到过一个我很喜欢的合作公司的例子。我们合作了一段时间后，有一月份我们查看了数据，发现新加入的供应商体验很糟糕。我们当时就想，"我们得做点什么。"（00:50:55）：于是我们决定开发一些定制功能，引导他们与市场另一端更有经验的人合作。效果不错。但随后我们发现，那些现有供应商的体验反而更差了。（00:51:12）：这真让人左右为难。我们又想，"等等，我们得解决这个问题。"于是我们把他们和更有经验的人匹配起来。一个月后，情况又反转了。（00:51:24）：这是因为市场管理的博弈本质上就是在重新分配注意力和资源。有时你运气好能为所有人创造更大的蛋糕。但我认识的Upwork前CFO、后来加入Thumbtack的Servaes Tholen说过一句让我难忘的话："经营市场平台时，你必须意识到许多关键决策都会产生赢家和输家。要应对这些变化，就得判断你创造的赢家对业务的价值，是否比过程中产生的输家更重要。" 这是一个残酷的现实，因为没人愿意承认某项功能调整会损害市场中某些参与者的利益。但由于市场平台运作的根本约束，许多我们选择实施的调整及其引发的资源重新分配，短期内未必能创造显著的收益增长。你往往会押注于某个方向，而当前的资源重新分配就是你下注的方向。（00:52:30）：所以Superhost让我感兴趣的地方在于，它在一定程度上启发我们思考：如果要从短期视角定义一个能捕捉这种权衡的指标，应该如何设置？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great way to think about it. I wanted to come back to this idea you're sharing of maybe you should run experiments more quickly, not wait for stat sig, have a culture of learning versus impact. In practice, it's very difficult, because people are measured by impact. There's performance reviews, there's promotions, there's how much impact did this team drive, are going to look at their experiment results? You've worked with a lot of marketplace companies, a lot of different companies. Is there anything you've seen about something you could do to help the company shift and actually work this way, while also recognizing success, and who's doing great, who's not, which team's driving impact, who's not?
turns.zh: 这样想真是太棒了。我想再谈谈你提到的这个观点——或许你应该更快地开展实验，而不是等待统计显著性结果，营造一种重视学习而非追求立竿见影效果的文化。但在实际操作中，这非常困难，因为人们的绩效往往以成果为衡量标准。绩效评估、晋升机会、团队创造的价值大小……这些标准都与实验结果息息相关。你与许多市场型公司和不同类型的企业合作过，有没有什么经验可以帮助企业转变思维方式，真正践行这种理念，同时还能有效识别成功案例、评估表现优劣，以及明确哪些团队在创造价值、哪些团队尚有提升空间？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Interestingly, it's actually an active area of research for me now. What I mean by active area of research is I care a lot about the incentives that we create for data science through how we set up reward mechanisms. So there's a couple things I think that could be helpful, that are maybe there may be a little bit less about... Maybe I'm not going to directly answer the question you ask, because I think that's a hard one, right? I think I recognize that measurement on impact is critical. Well, let me answer that actually from the most obvious way first. I think there's a cultural issue here that's really critical. (00:53:56): One of the things I often find is that my PhD students, our PhD students here often go off and get great data scientist jobs. And in one sense, they're doing amazing stuff. They apply really technically sophisticated methods. But when I look at the problems they're working on, they're often more at the margins of the business than they should be. (00:54:13): And it's a cultural thing. It's basically because if you're measured narrowly on impact and that's all anyone sees around you, then it's very hard to engage with the creative aspect of business change and the strategic aspects of business change. (00:54:26): So the cultural aspect there is, I think it's partly incumbent on the leaders to expect something more of their data scientists. And what I mean by expect more is that you expect them to do more than deliver narrowly defined, statistically rigorous results to you in their reports. You're actually expecting them to talk also about what they're learning about the business in the process. So where that's headed is there's this concept of being hypothesis driven, which is like the technical phrase. What does that mean? Again, in a more lay sense. (00:54:58): What it means is tests aren't going to be defined only in terms of winners and losers, that each test should also say something about what will we learn about a business flow, a funnel, preferences of the guests, preferences of the hosts. What will we learn about their demand elasticity if we're changing prices around? These kinds of things. So it's possible to articulate in an experiment doc, a launch doc, what are the hypotheses that are being tested? So that's one thing I would say is just culturally, setting the norms that learning is part of the discourse, and it's expected actually I think is important. (00:55:33): But the other thing I would say that's maybe a little bit more about programmatically, what could a data science platform team do? A funny thing about experiments is that we throw past learning away effectively. And this is just an artifact of how we analyze experiments, that the statistical methods used typically, P-values, confidence intervals, these fall into a branch of statistics known as frequentist statistics. And the idea behind frequentist statistics without being overly technical is just I let the data speak for itself. There's no beliefs brought to the table about where that data came from. (00:56:10): But if you think about this in a company, in A/B testing a company, it's a weird thing, right? Because I might've run 1,000 A/B tests in the past on this exact same button, or call to action, or color, and now I am going to completely ignore that and focus only on this. (00:56:23): So there's ways to take the past into account, to build what's called a prior belief before I run an experiment, and now take the data from the experiment, connect it with the prior, to come up with a conclusion of, "Okay, in light of the past plus this experiment, what's it telling me about the future?" And that falls broadly under the category of what's called Bayesian A/B testing. (00:56:46): So that's one of the things I think can help culturally, weirdly. It's a super technical thing, but I think it can help culturally, because what it's doing is it's now rewarding people for contributing information to that prior. And I think it then becomes possible to say, "Your experiment that failed actually moved our prior." And that's an important thing, because by doing so, you're now altering how we're going to think about this flow or this pricing plan in all future experiments. (00:57:14): So there's an information positive externality, positive network effect that's generated for the rest of your business if I can somehow encode what you learned into the analysis of future experiments. So this is one thing. There's strong connection between the culture and incentives of A/B testing and the ability to actually incorporate past learning into these prior beliefs.
turns.zh:
很有趣的是，这对我来说现在是一个活跃的研究领域。我所说的活跃研究领域是指，我非常关注我们通过设置奖励机制为数据科学创造的激励机制。因此，我认为有几点可能会有所帮助，虽然这些可能与您的问题关系不大……或许我不会直接回答您的问题，因为我认为这确实是个很难回答的问题，对吧？我认为衡量影响力至关重要。嗯，让我先从最明显的方面来回答。我认为这里存在一个非常关键的文化问题（00:53:56）。我经常发现，我的博士生，我们这里的博士生毕业后往往能找到很棒的数据科学工作岗位。从某种意义上说，他们做得非常出色。他们应用了非常复杂的技术方法。但当我观察他们正在处理的问题时，这些问题往往处于业务边缘，而不是应该处于核心位置。（00:54:13）这是一个文化问题。根本原因是，如果仅从狭隘的角度衡量影响力，并且这是周围人唯一看到的标准，那么就很难参与到业务变革的创造性方面和战略性方面。（00:54:26）所以文化层面的问题在于，我认为领导者有责任对数据科学家有更高的期望。我所说的更高的期望是指，您期望他们不仅仅是在报告中提供狭隘定义的、统计严谨的结果。您还期望他们在过程中谈论他们对业务的了解。因此，目标是形成假设驱动的文化，这是技术术语。什么意思呢？用更通俗的话来说，这意味着测试不应仅限于胜负判断，每个测试还应揭示我们将了解到哪些关于业务流程、漏斗、客人偏好、房东偏好的信息。如果我们调整价格，我们将了解到他们的需求弹性如何？这些都是可以量化的。因此，可以在实验文档、发布文档中明确说明正在测试哪些假设。所以我要说的一点是，从文化层面出发，设定学习是讨论的一部分，我认为这很重要。（00:55:33）但我要说的另一件事可能更偏向于程序层面，数据科学平台团队可以做些什么？关于实验的一个有趣之处是，我们有效地忽略了过去的经验。这只是我们分析实验的一种副作用，通常使用的统计方法——P值、置信区间——属于频率主义统计学。频率主义统计学的核心思想（不做过多技术解释）就是让数据自己说话，不带入任何关于数据来源的先验信念。（00:56:10）但如果您在一家公司考虑A/B测试，这就很奇怪了，对吧？因为我可能过去在同一个按钮、行动呼吁或颜色上运行过1000次A/B测试，现在却完全忽略这些，只专注于这次测试。（00:56:23）因此，有办法考虑过去的经验，在运行实验前建立所谓的先验信念，然后结合实验数据与先验信念，得出结论：“好的，鉴于过去的经验加上本次实验的数据……”
主持人："通过这次实验，您能告诉我关于未来的哪些信息？" 这基本上属于贝叶斯A/B测试的范畴。（00:56:46）：所以我认为这在文化层面能产生积极影响，虽然听起来有些奇怪。这是一项极具技术性的方法，但我认为它能对文化产生积极影响，因为它现在会奖励那些为先验概率提供信息的人。我认为这样一来，我们就能说"你那次失败的实验实际上改变了我们的先验概率"。这很重要，因为通过这样做，你正在改变我们在未来所有实验中对这一流程或定价方案的思考方式。（00:57:14）：所以，如果我能将你学到的知识编码到未来实验的分析中，就能为你的整个业务创造信息正外部性和积极的网络效应。这就是其一。A/B测试的文化与激励机制与将过去的经验教训融入先验信念的能力之间存在着紧密的联系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you're doing research in this area. We should bring you back when you've completed it and have the ultimate answer for everyone to change how they operate.
turns.zh: 我很高兴你正在这个领域进行研究。等你完成研究，得出最终结论时，我们应该邀请你回来，让所有人都能借此改变自己的工作方式。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah, one of the great things about professors is we never complete anything and never have ultimate answers.
turns.zh: 是啊，当教授的好处之一就是我们永远做不完事，永远找不到最终的答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh boy.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah, I'll do my best though.
turns.zh: 是的，我会尽力而为的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on a really interesting concept that you shared with me around how, just learning isn't free. People think that they could just learn a bunch of stuff and there's not a cost to it. I'd love for you to just chat a bit about what that means.
turns.zh: 你之前和我分享的一个观点非常有趣，那就是学习本身并非免费。人们总以为学点东西没什么成本。我很希望你能稍微聊聊这意味着什么。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Let me start with an anecdote, that I just absolutely love this anecdote. I use it every year in class. So I was talking to a real estate platform, and they had a marketing data science manager who's basically responsible, as many marketing managers are, for allocation of ad spend across different channels. (00:58:22): And what they discovered had happened at the end of the year is in one hand, the team had done great, but the manager had held out some subset of arriving visitors, not showing them any of the innovations they were making.
turns.zh: 让我先讲个趣闻，我特别喜欢这个故事，每年上课时都会拿它举例。当时我和一个房地产平台的负责人交流，他们有个市场数据科学经理，跟很多市场经理一样，主要负责在不同渠道分配广告投放预算。（00:58:22）结果年底盘点时，发现团队虽然表现出色，但这位经理却故意藏了一批访客数据，没有向他们展示团队推出的创新成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like a holdout group?
turns.zh: 藏起一批数据？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. What's called a holdout group in experimentation. And one thing about this holdout is it wasn't authorized. That's not the way things are supposed to work. They've got their ad spend, allocate out your ad spend, great. So at the end of the year, they looked at the hole out and they're like, "Wow, that cost us a couple million dollars, something in that range, and it's not a trivial amount of money. What's the deal? What were you thinking?" Basically. And of course the answer was, "Well, I get that I cost you that much, but number one, now you know what my team's worth. And number two, you would never have had that answer unless I'd done that on my own." (00:59:16): Now, why is that so powerful? I think what I find so interesting about experiments is that when you don't know something, it seems not even a question that you would allocate some of your samples to all options, right? Treatment and control. I have two different ways of doing something. I don't know which one's better, so of course I'll give some samples to each. After the fact you're like, "Treatment was better. What the heck were we thinking? Why'd we give all those samples to control? That doesn't make any sense now." There's this great Seinfeld clip where he mentions getting a bill at the end of a large luxurious meal, and people stare at the bill like, "We're not hungry now. Why'd we order all this food?" So it's the same thing. I mean, you know treatment's better now. Why'd you waste all those samples on control? (00:59:59): And I think that is such a powerful observation that you have to put yourself in the frame of reference of when you didn't have the answer. And at that moment, what you're essentially saying to yourself is that it's worth paying to learn the answer. I think it sounds obvious the way we're saying it now, or this anecdote of the marketing manager and the holdout sounds obvious. What's culturally not baked in I think is that idea. And the reason I say it's not culturally baked in, by the way, is because of the language of winners and losers. Because if we use that language, we're implicitly saying is that we wasted time when we ran an A/B test on loser. If I reward you for shipping winners, then what I'm really telling you is all the time that you spent testing out failures was wasted time. (01:00:46): And I think, of course, you don't want to keep data scientists around who regularly are just generating failures. That's not my point. (01:00:54): But my point is there's a disconnect there. On one hand, we can all look at the story of this marketing manager and chuckle at it. And yet, every day we're instantiating language and processes that are reinforcing that same theme, which is essentially trying to say to you, "If you're wasting samples on things that don't ultimately end up being a winner, then the act of doing so is a failure." (01:01:16): So I really feel that that idea that you have to pay to learn, again, it's a cultural thing, but it's also an education issue for businesses are populated by people of all stripes. Not everybody comes from a data science or experimentation background. And this idea that learning is costly is not natural, actually. It's not natural as a matter of human nature. It's certainly not natural as a matter of running a business.
turns.zh:
是啊，没错。这在实验中被称为"保留组"。而这次保留组的问题在于它是未经授权的。这根本不符合正常流程。他们已经分配了广告预算，分配了你的广告支出，这没问题。但年底回顾时，他们发现这项保留组花费了数百万美元——这可不是个小数目。他们就问："怎么回事？你当时在想什么？"基本上就是这样。对方当然会回答："我知道这花了你们这么多钱，但首先，现在你们知道我的团队有多值钱了。其次，如果我不自己做这项实验，你们根本得不到这个答案。"

（00:59:16）：那为什么这点如此重要？我觉得实验最有趣的地方在于，当你对某件事不确定时，人们通常会把样本分配给所有选项——比如实验组和对照组。我不知道哪个更好，当然就各给一点。但事后你会想："实验组效果更好。我们当时到底在想什么？为什么把所有样本都给了对照组？这太不明智了。"Seinfeld有一段经典桥段，讲的是在享用豪华大餐后，人们盯着账单疑惑："我们现在不饿了，为什么要点这么多？"道理是一样的。现在你知道实验组效果更好了，为什么还要把样本浪费在对照组上？

（00:59:59）：我认为这种认知转换非常重要，你必须设身处地地想想自己当初没有答案时的处境。那个时候，你其实是在告诉自己："为了得到答案，付出成本是值得的。"现在我们把这句话说得理所当然，或者用营销经理和保留组的例子来解释，听起来也很直观。但我觉得这种文化层面的认知并没有被广泛接受。究其原因，关键在于胜者和败者的语言框架。因为如果用这种语言框架，我们就默认在对失败者进行A/B测试是浪费时间。如果奖励成功者，那就是在告诉你，测试失败者的所有时间都是白费的。

（01:00:46）：当然，你肯定不希望身边有只会生成失败案例的数据科学家。这不是我的重点。（01:00:54）但重点在于这里存在脱节。一方面，我们看着营销经理的故事会觉得好笑。另一方面，我们每天都在使用强化这种文化的语言和流程，本质上是在告诉你："如果你把样本浪费在最终不成功的事情上，那就是失败的。"

（01:01:16）：所以我真的觉得，"为了学习而付费"这个观念，既是文化层面的问题，也是企业教育问题。毕竟企业里形形色色的人，不见得都来自数据科学或实验领域。学习需要付出成本，这并不自然。就人性而言，这不自然。从商业运营角度看，这更不自然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that example of the real estate platform where it's very viscerally, clearly cost. They lost because they didn't roll out experiments to this group for a long time. Such a good example of this idea in action. (01:01:55): You mentioned star ratings. I know you spent a lot of time on designing rating systems. Sorry, I didn't mean to imply star ratings. That's just one implementation. Rating systems in general. (01:02:05): So maybe just to keep it focused, say a marketplace founder is trying to decide and design how they do ratings, and reviews, and things like that. What's a couple pieces of advice you'd give them for how to do this correctly? And is there a model marketplace you'd point them to like, "These guys really do it really well"? And I know it's super specific based on the marketplace, but is there one just like, "They really nailed it"?
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢那个房地产平台的案例，它把成本问题呈现得非常直观、清晰。他们之所以失败，是因为很久没有针对这个群体开展实验。这真是这个理念在实践中的绝佳范例。（01:01:55）：你提到了星级评分系统。我知道你花了大量时间设计评分系统。抱歉，我不是指星级评分本身，那只是其中一种实现方式，而是指评分系统整体。（01:02:05）：那或许我们可以更聚焦一点。比如说，一个市场平台的创始人正试图决定如何设计评分、评论等功能。你能给他们一些正确做法的建议吗？有没有你认为做得特别出色的市场平台案例，可以推荐给他们？我知道这取决于具体的市场类型，但有没有某个平台能称得上是“典范案例”呢？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Oh man, that's a tough one. I think I'll answer the second part first. I don't feel like anyone's really nailed this. Yeah, I think there's a lot of innovation that's happened, but I think fundamentally, we're still playing with the same kind of tools that we had when eBay and Amazon first started thinking about how to do rating systems ages ago. (01:02:48): And part of the reason we haven't nailed it is because there's a lot of dynamics in play that lead to what's called rating inflation, where if you look at ratings over time in the marketplace... One of my colleagues, John Horton, who was a professor at MIT and has worked very closely with Upwork, we worked together when I was at oDesk, he was the staff economist there. He's written a couple of really nice papers with this empirical phenomenon that over time, you see the median rating inflating, let's say on marketplaces like oDesk, like Uber, like any of these. (01:03:16): And there's a lot of reasons for this, but one of them is just that there's a reciprocity issue, which is it's effectively, from your perspective, it's kind of costless if someone says to you, "Hey, please leave me a nice rating." And if you're seeing them or you're interacting with them, most people don't want to be mean. So that happens. (01:03:35): But there's another aspect of it, which is norming. As the ratings in the marketplace go up, they get normed, so that now you're in a condition, you're like, "A four star rating. I'm really screwing this person over." Whereas maybe when the marketplace started, you didn't think that. (01:03:47): So definitely one thing that we worked on in our research was to think about renorming, the meaning of some of these labels. And renorming could mean something like rather than the star ratings just being poor to excellent, the top rating has actually exceeded expectations. You could go one step further and you could say, "How did this compare to this experience you had in the past that you rated really highly?" And Airbnb had something like this in place, where they would actually ask you to compare, or ask you questions about expectations. (01:04:19): I find that that's really valuable because it's easier for people to say, "That was good but didn't exceed my expectations. That was good, but definitely not better than this amazing stay I had two months ago," than it is to say, "Well, I'm going to ding this person and give them four stars." So that's one issue. (01:04:36): And I think another thing I want to point out for any marketplace founder is that something you want to be really careful about is the concept of averaging and whether are the implications of averaging. And that's because a default for many marketplaces is to just average the ratings that people get. It feels very natural, right? Lenny's got five ratings, let me average them. (01:04:57): And that actually has some pretty important distributional consequences for the marketplace. Distributional in the sense of who wins, who loses. And that's because if you're averaging and you're really established on a platform, think of a restaurant on Yelp with 10,000 reviews, it's irrelevant what the next review is. It doesn't matter. Nothing's moving it at that point. (01:05:17): If you're new and you break into that market, and your first review is negative, you might be completely screwed. In fact, there's some early work on eBay that showed that if your first rating's negative, that could actually immediately cause an 8% hit on your immediate expected revenue, say nothing of long-term consequences. Subsequent work has found that that's a significant indicator of potential exit from the platform, just because now it's very hard to find work. And some platforms do things like maybe they won't show your ratings until you've accumulated a few. (01:05:46): But in the end, this kind of distributional fairness aspect of averaging is pretty significant. And one of the recent papers that we've written is trying to get platforms to think a little bit about that. There's ways to address that interestingly, through the same concept of a prior. And the prior basically says hey, if someone comes into the marketplace and instead of averaging them, I average them together with a prior belief, then maybe what that prior belief does, it says, "Yeah, you got one negative rating, but maybe you got a little bit unlucky," and maybe my prior belief is something which actually pulls your rating up a little bit and allows me to still have you alongside others in the marketplace to give you a chance at getting work, getting rides, etc. (01:06:28): So I believe pretty strongly in this kind of distributional fairness element of designing rating systems. I think it's been understudied. And I'll say in general actually, I think rating systems are understudied, which to me is astonishing. Because the biggest change from those Agoras and Trajan's Market elements of those kinds of markets, to me the biggest change is that we get to see what happened with our matches. (01:06:52): So as a data scientist working on marketplaces, I feel like it's incredible that more of us don't spend our time thinking about what we're learning from the matches, and what these rating systems are telling us, and what the impact of that is on who wins and who loses in these markets, kind of thinking about the social implications of these things. So that's something I'm pretty passionate about.
turns.zh:
天哪，这问题真难。我想我还是先回答第二部分吧。我觉得目前还没人能真正解决这个问题。是啊，虽然有很多创新举措，但从根本上说，我们现在用的还是和eBay、亚马逊最初考虑评分系统时用的那些工具一模一样。（01:02:48）而我们没能解决这个问题的原因之一，是市场中存在许多动态因素，导致了所谓的"评分膨胀"现象。比如，你观察市场平台上的评分变化会发现，虽然评分中位数在上升，但这背后有很多深层原因，其中最重要的是互惠心理。别人请你给好评时，你可能觉得这没什么成本。但当你和对方互动后，大多数人都不想显得刻薄，所以这种行为就形成了。（01:03:16）还有另一个因素是规范效应。随着评分上升，标准也会随之提高。比如，在eBay刚起步时，人们可能觉得四星评分还不错，但现在却觉得不够。（01:03:47）我们研究中关注的重点之一，就是如何重构评分标准的意义。比如，不再用"一星到五星"来评分，而是将最高评分设定为"超出预期"。Airbnb就曾尝试让用户对比过往体验，询问他们的真实感受。（01:04:19）我发现这种方法很有效，因为人们更容易说"虽然不错，但没超出预期"，而不是简单地给四星。（01:04:36）另外，市场创始者需要注意平均评分的弊端。很多平台默认将用户评分平均化，这看似合理，但其实会带来严重的分配不公。例如，Yelp上一个有1万条评论的餐厅，平均评分对其影响微乎其微。但新入场的商家如果首条评论是负面评价，可能会彻底被淘汰。eBay早期研究表明，首条负面评价会导致预期收入立即下降8%，更不用说长期影响了。
研究发现，这往往是用户可能退出平台的重要信号，因为现在找工作变得非常困难。有些平台会采取措施，比如在用户积累一定评分后才显示其评分结果。（01:05:46）但归根结底，平均评分机制中所体现的分配公平性至关重要。我们近期撰写的一篇论文就试图促使平台重视这一问题。有趣的是，通过先验概率的概念可以有效解决这一问题。先验概率本质上是这样一个机制：当新用户进入平台时，如果不直接采用平均评分，而是将其与先验概率相结合，那么先验概率会认为“虽然你收到了一条负面评分，但可能是运气不佳”。这种先验概率实际上会提升用户的评分，让他们在平台上继续获得工作机会或接单机会。（01:06:28）我坚信评分系统设计中的分配公平性至关重要，但这一领域研究不足。总的来说，我认为评分系统研究不足，这让我感到惊讶。因为从古希腊市场到现代平台经济的最大变化在于，我们能够直接观察交易结果。（01:06:52）作为市场平台的数据科学家，我深感遗憾的是，我们中很少有人花时间思考从交易中获取的信息、评分系统传递的信号，以及这些因素对市场中赢家与输家影响的深层逻辑，更鲜有人关注其背后的社会意义。这正是我深切关注的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I also led the review system flows for a while at Airbnb, and one of the things I'm most proud of is launching what we call double-blind reviews where you don't see the other person's review until you leave your review. The intention was to create more honesty and more accurate reviews. (01:07:32): It turned out the biggest impact was review rate went up, because people get this email, "Ramesh left you a review. If you want to see it, should leave a review." And that really increased review rate, which gave us more data. And it was a really fun experiment to work on.
turns.zh: 我还在Airbnb负责过一段时间的评价系统流程，其中最令我自豪的事情之一，就是推出了所谓的“双盲评价”功能——在你提交评价之前，无法看到对方的评价。我们的初衷是通过这种方式提升评价的真实性和准确性。（01:07:32）结果发现，最显著的影响在于评价率的提升。用户收到邮件提示“拉梅什给您留下了评价，若想查看，请先提交您的评价”后，评价率显著提升，为我们提供了更多数据。这次尝试过程十分有趣。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: There's a great concept in the literature on rating systems called the sound of silence, which is this idea that there's a lot of information in ratings that are not left. So Steve Tadelis, who's a professor at Berkeley, he had a really nice paper with some folks at eBay talking about what they called effective percent positive, where rather than normalizing just by the ratings, they normalized by including ratings that weren't left. And what you found was this was much more predictive of downstream performance of a seller. So there's a lot of information in that lack of a response. So it's cool that you're able to get more of that out.
turns.zh: 学术文献中有一个关于评分系统的概念叫“沉默之声”，即未被留下的评价中蕴含着大量信息。伯克利大学教授史蒂夫·塔德利斯（Steve Tadelis）曾与eBay团队合作发表过一篇精彩论文，提出了“有效正向率”概念。他们不局限于根据已有评价进行标准化，而是将未被留下的评价也纳入计算。结果发现，这种方法能更准确地预测卖家的后续表现。可见，用户的沉默中也蕴藏着宝贵的信息。很高兴你们能挖掘出更多此类价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So much easier just to not leave a review than leave a bad review. Right? The downside to you is just much better. Oh man, marketplaces are so fascinating. I could see why a founder would want to be a marketplace founder, because it's just such an interesting space. And hearing your feedback of, no, you're not a marketplace founder. Let's think about the problem you're solving. And it might be a marketplace, might change people's minds. Also, I feel like there's a podcast episode in every topic we touched on. I know we just scratched the surface a lot of things. (01:08:52): I know you got to run. Before we get to our lightning round, is there anything else you wanted to highlight, touch on, leave people with that are maybe working on marketplaces, thinking about a marketplace?
turns.zh: 相比留下差评，人们更倾向于选择不留评。是吧？但不留评的危害也更小。天啊，市场平台真是太迷人了。我能理解创始人为何想成为市场平台的缔造者，因为这是一个极具挑战性的领域。听你说，你不是市场平台的创始人，而是要专注于解决问题。不过说不定听众中有人会因此重新审视市场平台的可能性呢。此外，我觉得我们谈到的每个话题都值得做成一期播客。我知道我们只是触及了冰山一角。（01:08:52）知道你要走了。在进入闪电问答环节之前，还有什么想强调、分享给正在研究市场平台或考虑创立市场的听众的见解吗？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: I think one of the high level points I would make, and like you said, there's an entire podcast in this topic, is that I think people want to imagine LMs and AI driven data science automating out large parts of what it means to do data science in industry. And I think that's probably the wrong perspective. In some mundane sense, that's true. It's easier for me to code than it used to be before. It's easier for me to develop visualizations than it used to be. I can make dashboards faster. So programmatically, I think it's true in some basic sense. (01:09:35): But what I believe pretty strongly, and I teach data science here, and my students are asked to use LMs and generative AI on a weekly basis on all their assignments. So I've got an up close and personal beat on this, but I believe very strongly actually is what AI has done for us is it's massively expanded the frontier of things we could think about our problem, hypotheses we could have, maybe things we could test. It's just an astronomical explosion of explanations, and ideas, and principle. (01:10:06): And I really think actually what that does is puts more pressure on the human, not less. I think it becomes more important for humans to be in the loop in interacting with these tools to drive the funneling down process of identifying what matters, at all levels. That ranges from you're carrying out a data scientific analysis, and now because you've got these tools, you can hypothesize 10 explanations, maybe 100 explanations. Which of those are you going to focus attention on? What are you going to tell other people to focus their attention on? To you're running experiments, used to have 10 creatives you're testing for a marketing campaign, you got 1,000 creatives, you're testing for that marketing campaign. Maybe that completely changes the game of what it means to run an experiment. What are you actually looking for now? How do you evaluate that you found something that was good enough? (01:10:52): And I think these questions are not getting enough attention. I think people are looking for the automated tool that really cuts the human out. But what I've seen so far, and again, who knows? By 2024, I might have a totally different answer for you. I don't think so. But at the moment, what I see is that humans have actually become far more important to the productive data science loop, not far less.
turns.zh: 我认为我要提出的一个关键观点——正如你所说，这个话题已经有了一整期播客来探讨——是人们往往希望将LM（大语言模型）和AI驱动的数据科学自动化视为能替代工业界数据科学的大部分工作。但我认为这种观点可能存在误解。从某种程度上说，这确实没错。编程对我来说比以前更容易了，制作可视化图表也更便捷了，创建仪表板的速度也更快了。所以从基础层面看，这种程序化观点确实成立。（01:09:35）但我深信这一点——我在这里教授数据科学，我的学生每周在所有作业中都要使用LM和生成式AI。因此我对此有切身的体会。但我坚信AI为我们带来的最大价值在于，它极大地拓展了我们思考问题、提出假设、验证猜测的边界。各种解释、思路和原理如雨后春笋般涌现。（01:10:06）但我认为这实际上给人类带来了更大的压力，而非减轻压力。人类与这些工具互动、推动识别关键问题的过程变得愈发重要，这在各个层面都至关重要。无论是进行数据科学分析时，面对十个解释假设，现在有了AI工具，可能就有一百个假设，你该把注意力集中在哪个假设上？又该引导他人关注哪个假设？还是在开展实验时，从10个创意测试到1000个创意测试，这或许彻底改变了实验运作的规则。如今你真正在寻找什么？又该如何评估找到的结果是否足够优秀？（01:10:52）我认为这些问题没有得到足够关注。人们总在寻找能完全排除人类参与的自动化工具。但就目前来看，我所见证的是，人类在数据科学生产循环中的重要性实际上远超以往。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such an important point. I feel like we need to add AI corner to this podcast where we always think about, how does AI impact what we're talking about on this podcast?
turns.zh: 这真是个重要观点。我觉得我们需要在播客中增设一个AI专栏，持续探讨AI如何影响我们在播客中讨论的内容。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah, I can see that. I totally see that.
turns.zh: 是啊，我完全明白你的意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, we might start doing that. Ramesh, with that, we've reached a very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Let's try to knock through them so you can go teach your class. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，我们或许可以开始这么做。拉梅什，接下来我们要进行一个激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题要问你，争取尽快完成，这样你就能去上课了。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: I am ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. What are two or three books you've recommended most to other people
turns.zh: 好的。你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: When it comes to books, I have one I love that I start with always, which is How to Lie with Statistics. It's a tiny book, Darrell Huff from 1954, which is just for anyone that likes data at any level, it's such a fun read. It's a great book. (01:11:55): The second thing I recommend to people, and actually this is true even for people who are not expert, is David Freedman was a statistician at Berkeley who passed away in the 2000s, early 2000s. His writing was fantastic in getting us to think hard about process. He was especially fond of what he called shoe leather statistics, where you rolled your sleeves up, you got on the ground, boots on the ground, really getting in there, really trying to understand your data. (01:12:27): His writing is fantastic, his explanations are fantastic. He has a few different books at different levels I think people would love reading. Most importantly, what I like about it is he puts such emphasis on driving evidence and understanding of your processes that generate data. And I find often, data scientists don't even look at examples. (01:12:44): So at oDesk, it meant are you looking at actual jobs, and what's actually going on in your product before you're trying to do data science on it? So I think that's a Freedman insight, Freedman mantra, and so his writing is great. (01:12:58): The last one I was going to mention has nothing to do with data science or anything. It's called Four Thousand Weeks by Oliver Burkeman. I'm not a huge self-help type person, but I really like this book a lot. I think it's a little bit stoic in its approach, like stoic philosophy. But the basic point is you're only on earth somewhere in the neighborhood of 4,000 weeks, and my wife and I have this term we call infinite Q, which is no matter what you think you get done on a given day, more stuff's going to just keep coming in. (01:13:26): And he basically says that recognizing that is liberating. Because once you recognize it, it doesn't matter what you do. You're always going to have too much to do. There's no point in stressing out about having too much to do. And just that small shift of mindset than puts a lot more attention on the usual thing people worry about, which is, where do I want to prioritize my time? So he has a great way of writing about it, some concrete rules of thumb to help manage that way of thinking. And yeah, I think it's a great book.
turns.zh:
谈到书籍，我有一本心头好，每次入手必选——《如何用数据撒谎》。这本1954年由达雷尔·赫夫（Darrell Huff）撰写的小书，适合任何对数据感兴趣的人，它读起来趣味十足，堪称佳作。（01:11:55）  
我推荐的第二本书，实际上对非专业人士也适用，那就是大卫·弗里德曼（David Freedman）的作品。他是伯克利大学的统计学家，于21世纪初去世。他的作品极其出色，能引导读者深入思考研究过程。他尤其推崇“鞋皮统计学”，即亲身实践、深入实地、真正理解数据的研究方法。（01:12:27）  
他的写作风格和解释方式堪称典范。他有多本不同层次的著作，相信读者都会爱不释手。最重要的是，他强调数据驱动和理解数据生成过程的逻辑。遗憾的是，数据科学家往往忽视这些基础知识。（01:12:44）  
在oDesk工作时，我曾强调：在进行数据科学研究前，是否真正了解产品实际情况和用户需求？这正是弗里德曼的洞见和智慧所在。（01:12:58）  
最后要提的是奥利弗·伯克曼（Oliver Burkeman）的《四千周》。我并非狂热的自助书籍爱好者，但这本著作让我深有共鸣。书中秉承斯多葛主义哲学，指出人生仅有约4000周的时间。与妻子共创的“无限Q”概念——无论你以为完成了多少工作，总有新任务接踵而至。（01:13:26）  
作者指出：意识到这一点是解脱。既然无法改变现状，何必为过多工作焦虑？这种思维转变能让人们更专注于优先分配时间。书中还提供了具体的实用建议，堪称佳作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近看过哪部喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: I am a climber, and one movie that I really liked was The Alpinist. I know a lot of people have seen Free Solo, but for anyone that kind of likes that genre, I would recommend they watch The Alpinist. (01:14:06): I think climbing is an interesting sport because has very much a psychological aspect of it. And I think that movie is pretty good at this meta level where you reflect a little bit on, what does it mean to make a movie about people who are obviously putting themselves into such risky situations? So I really enjoyed that. (01:14:25): On TV, we've been watching Only Murders in the Building, but I'm enough episodes behind right now that I probably won't say anything more, because I am trying to avoid any spoilers and I'm sure there's people out there trying to do the same. So great show though on Hulu.
turns.zh:
我是一名攀岩爱好者，《登山者》这部电影让我印象深刻。许多人看过《徒手攀岩》，但对这类题材感兴趣的人，我推荐《登山者》。（01:14:06）  
我认为攀岩是一项心理挑战极高的运动。这部电影在元叙事层面做得很好，引发观众反思：拍摄一部聚焦冒险者的电影，其意义何在？这让我深有共鸣。（01:14:25）  
电视剧方面，我们一直在追《致命校园》，但目前我落后了好几集，暂不剧透了，免得影响其他观众。不过这部Hulu平台的剧确实很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates that you're hiring?
turns.zh: 在面试候选人时，你最喜欢问的一个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: I interview people probably that are a little bit different than most of your podcast listeners. But that said, there's one question I like to ask a lot, and that's if you imagine... Often in our interviews in academia, whether it's grad students or faculty will ask people about their plans. (01:15:00): And what I like to ask people is, "Okay, now imagine everything works out, all the challenges you're facing work out, all your plans work out, everything hits the top end of your vision for what this could be. What do you imagine is the impact of having done that? Who's being impacted by that? Why is that a big deal that happened?" (01:15:20): And I find that's a really valuable question to ask, because first of all, many people haven't thought about that. We're so short-term focused, we don't even think, "Boy, if everything worked out, what would be the big deal because of what I did?" Startup founders tend to be better at this than most people obviously. (01:15:35): But another reason I like it is because you will find in that conversation that their vision expands a little bit of additional spheres that are touched or impacted by what they're thinking about doing. So on both sides, it's kind of a revealing question, I think. So I find that important for my line of work, but my hunch is that might be useful for some of your listeners too.
turns.zh: 我采访的人可能和你们大多数播客听众不太一样。不过说真的，我经常会问一个问题：如果你想象一下……在学术界的采访中，无论是研究生还是教职员工，都会问人们关于他们的计划。（01:15:00）而我喜欢问人们的是：“好吧，现在想象一切顺利，你面临的所有挑战都解决了，你的所有计划都实现了，一切都达到了你对其潜力的最高预期。你想象这样做会有什么影响？谁会受到影响？为什么这件事会如此重要？” （01:15:20）我发现这是一个非常有价值的问题，首先，很多人从未想过这些。我们太注重短期目标了，甚至不会想：“天哪，如果一切顺利，我所做的事会带来什么重大影响？” 创业者显然比大多数人更擅长这个。（01:15:35）但我喜欢这个问题的另一个原因是，在对话中，你会发现他们的愿景会扩展到更多与他们所考虑的行动相关的领域。因此，从双方来看，这都是一个很有启发性的问题。我认为这对我的工作很重要，但我觉得这对你们的一些听众可能也很有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, such a unique perspective on interviewing, versus most of the guests that I interview in tech company.
turns.zh: 是啊，这是一个独特的采访视角，与我采访的大多数科技公司嘉宾不同。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah, normally there's a coding question, right? I should say I would never ask a coding question post November 2022 after we got AI to help us code. I think it's a superpower.
turns.zh: 是啊，以前通常会问编程问题，对吧？我得说，在2022年11月我们让AI帮我们写代码之后，我再也不问编程问题了。我觉得这简直是个超能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: AI corner. What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: AI专区。你最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: I also really like cycling. And I'm not ashamed to admit that I think that e-bikes are the greatest thing for cycling. Admittedly, I'm late forties, so maybe I'm the right target demographic too. But yeah, I love my e-road bike. It's great, because it's not one of those with a throttle, you have to work, but it kicks in just when you're on your sixth hill and you don't want to go up the last hill anymore on the way home. So yeah, that's amazing. I think that's just transformative for people that like cycling, but have busy lives. (01:16:51): And I think another one that my son who's 10 roped me into actually, is we were in Santa Cruz browsing at a kitchenware shop of all places, and he saw an outdoor pizza oven, a tiny portable one. And he just did research for two weeks and insisted we get one. (01:17:07): So he got one over the summer, and after we got it, he refused to eat pizza out anymore as a 10-year-old. So maybe that's the best thing I could say about the quality of pizza you can get from a home outdoor portable pizza oven.
turns.zh: 我也非常喜欢骑自行车。我毫不羞愧地承认，我认为电动自行车是骑行的最佳选择。诚然，我已经四十多岁了，所以也许我也是合适的目标人群。但是的，我是喜欢电动公路自行车。这很棒，因为它不是那种有油门的类型，你得自己动手，但当你在回家路上爬第六个山坡，而你不想再爬最后一个山坡时，它就会启动。所以是的，这太棒了。我认为这对喜欢骑行但生活忙碌的人来说是革命性的。（01:16:51）还有一个是我10岁的儿子拉我入坑的，我们在圣克鲁斯随便逛一家厨房用品店，他看到了一个户外披萨烤箱，一个小小的便携式的。他花了两周时间研究，最后坚持要我们买一个。（01:17:07）今年夏天我们买了之后，他就不再想出去吃披萨了。所以也许这是我能说的最好的关于在家使用便携式户外披萨烤箱能得到的披萨质量的评价。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God, I'm hungry. I am going to go have to get some pizza now. What is a favorite life motto that you like to repeat to yourself, share with folks, find useful in your day-to-day?
turns.zh: 天哪，我饿了。我现在得去吃点披萨了。你有什么喜欢的座右铭，喜欢对自己重复，喜欢和别人分享，觉得在日常生活中很有用的？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: A lot of my work involves talking to students of all stripes. And I guess these students go on to be data scientists, go on to be founders, and a lot of them go in the tech industry. So maybe in that sense, that advice is relevant. (01:17:43): My main thing I tell people is slow down. I think what I've found has been happening, is we're so convinced that speed is the way you're going to find the right answer, that I just don't think we slow down to develop meaningful mental models of the things we're doing. That's certainly true in the research projects I work on. It's consistently true when I talk to people in business, and I ask them about their... By mental model, I just mean if you're running a marketplace, what is your model of what people care about? What makes people stay versus leave? What makes matches work versus not work? All those things shape a roadmap in your mind. And I think a lot of roadmapping, a lot of execution, paper writing in academia has all just become far more fast-paced, at the expense of deeper thinking about these kinds of structural features of the thing you're building. (01:18:41): So with my students, but also I think with people I interact with in industry, I think slowing down is actually more of a virtue than it's given credit for.
turns.zh: 我的许多工作都需要与形形色色的学生交流。我猜这些学生后来成为了数据科学家、创业者，或者投身科技行业。所以从这个角度来看，那些建议或许还是有价值的。（01:17:43）：我最常给人们的建议是放慢脚步。我发现一个普遍现象，那就是我们太执着于用速度来寻找正确答案，以至于我们没有时间去建立对所做事情的深刻理解模型。在我参与的研究项目中尤其如此。与商界人士交流时也是如此——当我问他们……这里所说的"心理模型"指的是，如果你运营一个市场平台，你对用户关心的核心诉求有何理解？是什么因素让用户留存或流失？什么因素能促成匹配成功或失败？所有这些要素共同构成了你心中的路线图。我认为很多路线规划、执行过程，以及学术界的论文写作，都因追求速度而牺牲了对所构建事物结构性特征的深度思考。（01:18:41）：所以无论是面对学生，还是与商界人士交流，我都认为放慢脚步其实是一种被低估的美德。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very similar to a motto that a recent guest shared, which I think was go slow to go fast, or stay smooth to go fast.
turns.zh: 这和最近一位嘉宾分享的座右铭很相似，叫做"慢即是快"，或者"保持平稳才能快速前进"。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah, I like that. Maybe I'll pilfer that, when I go talk to my grad students [inaudible 01:19:03].
turns.zh: 是啊，我很喜欢这个说法。或许我该借用一下，在给研究生做讲座时用用（01:19:03）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You're a professor at Stanford University, which sounds incredibly cool. What's something about being a professor at Stanford in particular or in general that would surprise people, either good or bad?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你是斯坦福大学的教授，听起来非常了不起。关于在斯坦福当教授，有什么特别之处或普遍特点，无论好坏，都可能让人们感到惊讶？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, we've had a rough ride, as everybody probably knows. Stanford's been in the news for a lot of not so great reasons, I think over the last five years especially. (01:19:29): So I don't know if this is the right kind of surprise, but I think one thing that I find really energizing at Stanford is people have never asked me for credentialing here. And what I mean by that is that I came from a bunch of other good schools, and obviously I've spent time in industry with a lot of great companies. And a kind of cultural dynamic that can often develop is, "Well, before I'm going to talk to you, I want to know something about why you're worth talking to. Give me your credentials. Where are you a grad student or where are you a professor? Tell me about yourself first." (01:20:10): One of the things that I found very surprising when I came here is just how that never happened at any level. Grad students tell me this all the time. Go talk to someone across campus and just launch right into a conversation about how your X meets my Y, and we have something we could do together. As a faculty member, it happens all the time. I just had a conversation a couple days ago with someone about effectively a marketplace of experiment designs for nano fabrication here, which is totally out of left field for things I do, and yet seamless. Our conversation was about the substance rather than the credentialing. (01:20:46): I really think part of the reason for that is that Stanford is sort of unique in that it doesn't have a weakness across the board. We have strong professional schools, law, business, medicine, strong engineering schools, strong humanities and social sciences. And then that and the weather is what I usually tell people honestly, which matters a lot. People are willing to walk anywhere. I think those things combine to create a culture and an environment where you don't credential everybody. (01:21:09): And I think that means a lot. I think that's something that I haven't found elsewhere. And if people wanted to know something about what's Stanford's like on the inside, I think that's one aspect of it that probably isn't discussed very much. I think that's part of what makes it really fun to be here.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，我们这几年过得挺坎坷的，想必大家都知道。过去五年，斯坦福大学频频登上新闻头条，原因大多不怎么光彩。（01:19:29）所以我不知道这算不算意外的惊喜，但我觉得在斯坦福最让我振奋的一点是，这里的人从不以资历来评判我。我的意思是，我曾就读于其他许多优秀学府，也在业界与众多顶尖公司共事过。通常会形成的一种文化动态是：“嗯，在跟你交谈之前，我得先了解你为何值得交流。请先亮明你的资历。你是研究生还是教授？先自我介绍一下吧。” （01:20:10）来到这里后，我发现最惊喜的一点是，这种评判从上到下都压根不存在。研究生们总是跟我这么说。你去校园里找人聊天，直接就能展开对话——比如你的X技术如何与我的Y技术契合，我们可以一起做些什么。作为教员，这种情况也屡见不鲜。前几天我还和人聊了这里的纳米制造实验设计市场，这完全超出我的专业范畴，但交流却顺畅自然。我们谈论的是实质内容，而非资历证明。 （01:20:46）我觉得部分原因在于斯坦福独一无二——它没有哪个方面是薄弱的。我们有实力强劲的专业学院，比如法学院、商学院、医学院，还有实力出众的工程学院和人文社科院系。说实话，我常跟人说天气也是一大亮点——人们愿意步行去任何地方。这些因素共同营造了一种文化和环境，让人们无需过多强调资历来证明自己。 （01:21:09）这意义非凡。我觉得这在其他地方很难找到。如果有人想了解斯坦福的内部情况，我觉得这方面鲜少被提及。这或许正是这里最有趣的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's also an incredibly dreamy campus, that is very joyful to walk around. That helps, I'm sure. Ramesh, I feel like we got people's brains tingling. I think we've created new marketplace founders, and also convinced people maybe they aren't marketplace founders. So maybe we netted out zero new marketplace founders. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 这里的校园也美得令人沉醉，漫步其中令人心旷神怡。这无疑也是一大助力。拉梅什，我觉得我们成功激发了听众的兴趣。我觉得我们培养了新的市场平台创始人，也让一些人意识到自己或许并非市场平台创始人。所以或许我们最终没新增多少市场平台创始人。最后两个问题。若想联系您，听众该去哪里找您？听众又如何能为您提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: I think the easiest way, if someone's interested more on the industrial side is probably LinkedIn. You send me a message or connect there. Also, because I'm an academic, I have my own Stanford webpage, and it's pretty easy to figure out how to find me there as well. (01:22:02): And how can listeners help me? I kind of feel the most important thing that someone listening to this could do is take forward some of the messages that came out in terms of what it means to be data literate. And I think there's a lot you can do to educate yourself there. (01:22:18): Maybe one final thought I'll share is that in the same way that AI generates a lot of ideas, AI also generates a lot of prose. And in data science, that can actually be deadly because you're getting more explanations that sometimes maybe are extraneous. (01:22:35): So taking that as a little vignette, I think that what the world needs is data literacy on the part of people interacting with these tools and with each other. So that's the thing I care most about. The things I teach, the things I do research on, they're all connected to that theme. And so that's where I'm pretty excited. I do work with companies regularly, and so if there's interesting opportunities that fall in the sphere of stuff we've discussed on the podcast, always happy to listen.
turns.zh: 我认为，如果有人对工业领域更感兴趣，最简单的方法可能是使用领英。您可以在那里给我发消息或建立联系。此外，因为我是一名学者，我在斯坦福大学有自己的网页，在那里找到我的方式也相当简单。（01:22:02）：听众如何能帮助我呢？我觉得听众能做的最重要的事，就是将节目中提到的数据素养含义进一步传播。我认为大家可以做很多事情来提升自身素养。（01:22:18）：最后我想分享一点：AI虽然能产生大量想法，但也会产生大量冗余内容。在数据科学中，这可能会带来致命影响，因为你会得到过多可能无关紧要的解释。（01:22:35）：以此为例，我认为世界最需要的是与这些工具互动的人们具备数据素养。这是我最关心的问题。我所教授的内容、从事的研究都与这一主题息息相关。这也是我最为兴奋的地方。我经常与企业合作，如果有与我们在播客中讨论的领域相关的有趣机会，我非常乐意倾听。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I think we've made a dent in helping people become a little more data literate. Ramesh, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我认为我们已经在帮助人们提高数据素养方面取得了进展。拉梅什，非常感谢你今天的到来。

turns.speaker: Ramesh Johari
turns.en: All right. Thank you so much, Lenny.
turns.zh: 好的，非常感谢你，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bye everyone. (01:23:11): Thank you so much for listening. If you found this valuable, you can subscribe to the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. Also, please consider giving us a rating or leaving a review, as that really helps other listeners find the podcast. You can find all past episodes or learn more about the show at lennyspodcast.com. See you in the next episode.
turns.zh: 大家再见。（01:23:11）：非常感谢您的收听。如果您觉得这期节目有价值，可以在Apple Podcasts、Spotify或您喜欢的播客应用上订阅节目。同时，欢迎给我们评分或留下评论，这对其他听众找到节目非常有帮助。您可以在l越来越多地了解播客。下期节目见。
